Periodic Table Observatory

· keys 1-9,0 tabs Space pause ←→ K
What this is & why it matters
Everything you eat, buy, build or sell is made from just 118 ingredients. The Periodic Table Observatory explains them through everyday life: your body, your home, your phone, your money and the night sky. It starts from zero (no science needed) and goes all the way to deep math. Every number is checked against public scientific data (PubChem, NIST, AME2020/NUBASE2020) and a 108-item fact-check ledger. It is hands-on, works offline in one file, and is built to grow with every question people ask. Start with 🎬 the slideshow, ❓ ask a question, or ✋ try it yourself. (Press E to hide these notes.)
← → arrow keys · Esc to skip
Level 0: from nothing to the findings, hands-onYou only need to read English. Mouse or finger both work. Press [ and ] to move between steps.
Each square is one kind of atom (one element). Every atom has a heavy middle, and even tinier specks called electrons zoom around it. The middle pulls on its specks a bit like a magnet pulls a paperclip. Ionization energy means how hard you must pull to take away the outermost speck. Helium holds on the tightest. Caesium holds on so loosely that it grabs at water and bursts into flame. Electronegativity means how strongly an atom pulls on specks it shares with a neighbour, like a tug-of-war.
Color by: COMPUTED from data
Red dot = Madelung exception (PubChem config differs from aufbau order). Gray = no value in source data.
Click an element.
This is the same map, rolled into a spring shape (a spiral), with one loop for each row of the map. Rows get longer as you go down (2, then 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 squares) because heavier atoms have more room for their specks. The spring shape is just for looking. The size of each dot is a real measurement.
3D periodic spiral (WebGL, written inline)LAYOUT = METAPHORvalues COMPUTED
Each turn of the helix is one period, and the angle is the position within that period. Height = period; colour = block; point size = the chosen property. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, hover for values. The spiral is a visual arrangement only; it carries no physics.
Size by:
Imagine fireflies blinking in a dark field, each at its own speed. When each one sees its neighbours, it nudges its own blinking a little toward theirs. Soon many blink together. A clapping crowd does the same thing. Here, every dot is one kind of atom, given a blink speed based on how tightly it holds its specks. The slider sets how strongly neighbours nudge each other. R is a togetherness score: 0 means everyone is blinking at random times, 1 means everyone blinks at the exact same moment. Honest result: the dots do fall into step, but the groups they form don't match the real families of atoms. So this game alone tells us nothing new about atoms.
Kuramoto on elementsCOMPUTED live
Oscillators = elements with IE, EN and radius. ω = standardized IE; coupling = exp(−d²) property similarity, row-normalized. Euler dt = 0.05.
R(t) =
Honest result (expand/corpus passes): R rises smoothly with K, and the phase clusters do not recover the blocks beyond the null. Taylor's printed R = 0.999437 is consistent with large K. It is a parameter choice, not a property of the elements.
Picture a row of 7 light switches, each either on or off. Any whole number can be written as such a row; computers store numbers this way, and the method is called binary. A code here simply means one row of switches. Hamming distance counts how many switches you'd have to flip to turn one row into another. Taylor's 48 codes turn out to be just the odd numbers from 3 to 97. The Fiedler split is a way to cut a web of connections into two groups while breaking as few links as possible, like splitting a class into two friend groups.
Hamming ring: Taylor's 48 odd masks 3..97COMPUTED live
Distance filter:

Masks 3..97 are exactly the odd atomic numbers Li..Bk, so "m48 = 97 = Berkelium" is true by construction. METAPHOR "doors", "vault"

The Fiedler vector is computed in-browser (Jacobi eigensolver on the normalized Laplacian of W = e−Hamming). The median split is 24/24 by construction and follows the high bits (Z < 64 vs ≥ 64), not chemistry.

An atom's specks sit at different distances from the middle, almost like rows of seats in a theatre. Each row holds a fixed number. Science books give one simple order for filling the seats, called the Madelung rule. 19 kinds of atom don't follow it: like a person who moves to a different row because it's more comfortable there. Each gate on this tab is a yes/no test that tries to explain why. All but one are explained. Neptunium is still a mystery, because the measurement needed to test it hasn't been recorded.
Two-gate admit/refuse on Madelung exceptionsCOMPUTED
Gate 1 = exact Madelung order (all exceptions are refused there). Gate 2 = half/full-shell rule. Gate 3 = a priori physics rule (thresholds partly informed by the data). LOO tree = leave-one-out decision tree. NIST LOO = leave-one-out model using the energy gaps of neighbouring elements (from NIST ASD).
The heavy middle of an atom is called the nucleus. It is a tight clump of even smaller bits held together by a powerful "glue". Binding energy is how much glue each bit gets. A star such as our Sun is a giant ball of glowing gas that squeezes small atoms together into bigger ones, and that gives off light and heat. This only pays off up to iron and nickel, the most tightly glued atoms. So stars can't make heavier atoms such as gold by squeezing; gold comes mostly from two dead stars crashing into each other. Magic numbers are counts of bits that make a "full set", which is extra stable. Odd-numbered atoms are rarer than even ones because the bits are steadier in pairs, like socks.
Binding energy per nucleon (AME2020, measured)COMPUTED
Shell gaps after magic N
Odd–even (Oddo–Harkins): solar vs crust
Superheavies Z = 104–118: longest-lived measured isotope
The island of stability (Z≈114/120/126, N≈184) is a prediction. The most neutron-rich nucleus measured has N = .
A scorecard. Every number printed on Taylor's original pictures was worked out again from real measurements. EXACT means it matched. CLOSE means nearly. WRONG means it didn't match. UNCHECKABLE means there was no way to test it.
Measurement ledger (all passes)COMPUTED

        💰 Money & Opportunity
        Every product, job and industry runs on these 118 ingredients. Here is where that turns into real value for ordinary people. Not financial advice. No prices, salaries or market sizes are shown, because those change and should come from a current, cited source.
        🛠️ Jobs built on elements
        • Electrician: works with copper wiring every day.
        • Battery technician / EV service: lithium, nickel and cobalt batteries.
        • Solar installer: silicon panels and copper and aluminium wiring.
        • Welder: joins steel (iron) and aluminium.
        • Radiology tech / nurse: X-ray and MRI scans that use iodine, barium, gadolinium and helium.
        • Jeweller: gold, silver and platinum.
        • Recycling and scrap yards: sorting copper, aluminium, steel and electronics.
        • Mining and metal processing.
        • Chip factory technician: silicon, copper, hafnium and ultra-pure gases.
        🏠 Everyday money ideas
        • Scrap metal: scrap yards buy copper, brass, aluminium and steel by weight; copper is usually worth far more per pound than steel.
        • E-waste: old phones and computers contain small amounts of gold, silver, copper and palladium; certified recyclers recover them.
        • Gold and silver are stores of value many people already understand (prices go up and down).
        • Knowing your chemistry saves money: baking soda and vinegar for cleaning, and never mixing bleach with ammonia (it makes a toxic gas).
        • Home energy: solar panels and efficient LED lighting can lower electricity bills.
        📈 Big trends shaping the next decade
        • Electric cars and home batteries are raising demand for lithium, nickel, cobalt and graphite (carbon).
        • Chips and AI: data centres need silicon chips, copper wiring and a lot of electricity.
        • Rare earths (neodymium, dysprosium) for magnets in motors and wind turbines; their supply chains are a major issue for governments.
        • Nuclear power (uranium) is getting renewed interest as a steady, low-carbon power source.
        • Recycling metals is growing as a way to secure supplies.

        What your body is made of (by weight, approximate textbook values)standard approximate values
        Sound and light are both waves: ripples that repeat, like ripples on a pond. This tab lets you pluck, hear, shine and look. Sound is off until you press a play button; set the volume here: . Every sound made from atom data is a sonification: we turn light measurements into notes you can hear. Atoms do not actually make these sounds.
        1 · Pluck a string: harmonicsSTRONG PARALLEL (same standing-wave math)
        Harmonic:
        A string fixed at both ends can only shake in whole-number patterns: 1 hump, 2, 3… Each pattern sounds a note at 1×, 2×, 3× the lowest pitch (here 110 Hz, the guitar's A string). An electron around an atom behaves like a wave that must "fit" too, which is why its energy comes in steps. One honest difference: a string's steps go as n, but hydrogen's energy goes as 1/n².
        2 · Hear the elementsSONIFICATION, not a real sound
        Hydrogen glows in four visible colours (NIST ASD, wavelengths in air): 656.28, 486.13, 434.05 and 410.17 nm. A nanometre (nm) is a millionth of a millimetre. We take each light wave's frequency and lower it by 40 octaves (divide by 2⁴⁰) so the note ratios stay true. Element chords use each element's 4 lowest NIST energy levels, turned into light frequencies and moved down whole octaves into hearing range. That keeps each note's letter name, but not its true octave.
        3 · Metronomes on a shared boardSTRONG PARALLEL (Kuramoto math)
        Metronomes standing on a board that can roll gently push the board, and the board pushes them back, until they tick together. A clapping audience falls into step the same way. Same equation as our Kuramoto tab.
        4 · Resonance in everyday lifereal effects
        🍷 Wine glass: sing exactly its natural note loudly enough and it shakes until it can crack.
        📻 Radio tuning: turning the dial picks the one station whose wave matches the circuit's natural rhythm.
        🧲 MRI scanner: hydrogen nuclei in your body spin like tiny tops in a strong magnet; radio waves at just the right rhythm make them answer back, and that echo builds the picture (real, and this is how hospitals see inside you).
        🍲 Microwave oven: its waves (2.45 billion wiggles a second) shake the water in food so it heats up. This is wave energy being absorbed, not a sharp resonance.
        5 · Light: prism and fingerprintsNIST ASD lines (air wavelengths)
        A prism spreads white light into a rainbow. Each element glows only in its own colours, like a barcode or fingerprint: sodium's yellow-orange glow (589 nm) lit old streetlights, and neon's red is neon signs. That's how we know what faraway stars are made of: we read their barcodes. Click a barcode to hear it (sonification).
        6 · Why gold is yellow and silver is whiteapprox. measured reflectance
        Drag the light ☀ around. Silver bounces back more than 90% of every colour, so it looks white. Gold bounces back over 90% of red and yellow but only about 40% of blue, so it looks yellow. The reason gold swallows blue is relativity: its fast inner electrons shift its levels. Metals are shiny because they have "free" electrons that can move around and send light straight back.
        7 · Shadows: seeing without seeingLOOSE ANALOGY for atoms
        Drag the light ☀. The closer the light is to the ball, the bigger the shadow; the size follows simple triangles. Scientists "see" atoms indirectly in a similar spirit: X-rays bounce off crystals and leave patterns of spots, and electron microscopes use beams of electrons. An eclipse is the Moon's shadow falling on Earth.

        Zoom of scale:
        The same patterns show up in everyday life. STRONG PARALLEL means scientists really use the very same calculations there. LOOSE ANALOGY means it's only a helpful comparison: it looks alike, but works differently underneath.
        Falling into step: fireflies, heartbeats, power lines, clappingSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Fireflies, clapping crowds, the cells that start each heartbeat, and the big machines that make electricity all slowly match their rhythm to their neighbours. Scientists describe all of them with the same formula, called the Kuramoto model. Our Kuramoto tab uses that same formula.
        Heartbeat cellsSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        A small patch of the heart holds about ten thousand cells. Each would beat at its own pace, but together they settle on one shared beat. That is your heartbeat. Same formula as the fireflies.
        Power lines staying in timeSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        The machines that make electricity for your home must all spin in time: in North America, 60 turns a second. If one drifts out of step, the lights can go out. The formula engineers use is a close cousin of the firefly formula.
        Atom seats ↔ theatre seatsLOOSE ANALOGY
        An atom's specks fill the closest free "seat" first, two to a seat. It helps you picture it, but real specks are blurry clouds, not people.
        Full sets: in the specks and in the middleSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Atoms with exactly 2, 10, 18, 36, 54 or 86 specks are calm and hardly react with anything. The middle of an atom is extra steady with 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82 or 126 bits. Both happen because a "layer" gets completely full. It's the same idea, but the layers fill in a different order.
        Cutting a web in two ↔ friend groupsSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Draw everyone in a school as dots, with a line between friends. The very same calculation as our Fiedler split is used by real apps to find friend groups, and to split up pictures and computer chips.
        Counting flipped switches ↔ QR codes, phones, DNASTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        A QR code is the square barcode your phone camera reads. It still works when scratched because it stores extra check-switches that spot and fix flips. Phones do the same with calls. DNA, the instruction book inside living things, is written in 4 letters; a mutation is a changed letter, counted the same way.
        Odd and even ↔ things are steadier in pairsSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        The bits inside an atom's middle are steadier in pairs. That's why atoms with an even count are more common than their odd neighbours. In the Sun this held every single time we checked (36 out of 36).
        Yes/no gates ↔ spam filters, teachers checking homeworkLOOSE ANALOGY
        A spam filter (the thing that hides junk email) runs a few yes/no checks in a row and only lets a message through if it passes. Our gates have the same shape, but the calculations inside are different.
        Glue curve ↔ why stars make iron and crashes make goldSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Stars shine by squeezing small atoms into bigger ones, which releases energy (energy means the ability to make light, heat or movement). That only works up to iron and nickel. Past that point, squeezing costs energy instead. Gold is made mostly when two collapsed stars crash together.
        Why gold is yellow and mercury is runny ↔ Einstein's speed rulesSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        In gold, the specks closest to the middle zoom at more than half the speed of light (light is the fastest thing there is). At that speed, Einstein's rules say they act heavier. That shifts the whole atom just enough that gold soaks up blue light and looks yellow. In mercury, the same thing makes it hold its outer specks so tightly that it stays liquid unless it is colder than about −39 °C, far colder than any freezer.

        Visual glossary

        Atom: one of the tiny pieces everything is made of
        Element: one kind of atom; there are 118 kinds
        Electron: a tiny speck zooming around the middle of an atom
        Nucleus: the heavy middle of an atom
        Ionization energy: how hard you must pull to steal an atom's outermost speck
        Shell: a "row of seats" for specks around the middle
        Madelung rule-breaker: an atom that fills its seats in an unusual order
        Togetherness score R: 0 means all out of step, 1 means perfectly together
        Hamming distance: how many on/off switches differ between two rows
        Fiedler split: cutting a web of links into two groups while breaking the fewest links
        Binding energy: how much "glue" each bit of an atom's middle gets
        Magic number: a count that makes a full, extra-steady set
        Odd-even rule: odd-numbered atoms are rarer than even ones
        Relativity effect: strange changes when things move close to the speed of light
        Ledger: a scorecard of checked facts
        Gate: a yes/no test
        The page checks its own homework: it adds up its totals again and makes sure they match the stored measurements. Green means they match.
        Self-check: every displayed total recomputed from the embedded data

# VALUE_MAP v2: what everyday people care about, and how the Observatory serves it

## 1. What people value (well-established principles)
| Principle | What it means for presentation | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Needs come in layers:** body and health, then safety, then belonging and family, then esteem and status, then growth and curiosity | Lead with health and safety, then family, then money, and save wonder for last | Maslow, A. H. (1943), "A Theory of Human Motivation", *Psychological Review* 50(4). The strict ordering is debated, but the categories are widely used |
| **Things about *me* are remembered better** (the self-reference effect) | Frame every topic as *your* body, *your* phone, *your* home | Rogers, Kuiper & Kirker (1977), *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 35(9) |
| **Stories pull people in and make ideas stick** (narrative transportation) | Open each slide with a short scene about a person: Maya shopping, Sam's phone, Rosa salting her steps | Green & Brock (2000), *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 79(5) |
| **Something that stands out gets remembered** (the isolation or von Restorff effect) | Use surprising facts: the iron in your blood came from a star; bananas are slightly radioactive | von Restorff (1933), *Psychologische Forschung* 18 |
| **Losses loom larger than equal gains** | Safety and avoiding harm (lead pipes, carbon monoxide) grab attention more than abstract benefits | Kahneman & Tversky (1979), "Prospect Theory", *Econometrica* 47(2) |
| **Attention must be earned quickly** (general principle; the "goldfish attention span" statistic is a myth and is not used here) | One question and one picture per screen, readable in about 5 seconds | General design principle |
| **Money, security and convenience** are everyday drivers | A Money & Opportunity tab with careers, recycling and trends; no invented numbers, not financial advice | General principle |
| **Curiosity is rewarding once basic needs feel covered** | End with wonder: stars, gold from star crashes, colours, sound | Same layering as above |

## 2. Each topic mapped to the value it serves
| Value | Observatory content |
|---|---|
| Health | Iron in your blood (made in stars); calcium and phosphorus in bones; iodine in salt; fluoride in toothpaste; your body is about 65% oxygen |
| Safety | Lead in old pipes; carbon monoxide alarms; smoke detectors (americium); never mixing bleach with ammonia |
| Family and home | Salt melting ice on the steps; why foil doesn't rust but the car does; pans with copper or aluminium bottoms; why a cut apple browns |
| Money and security | Phone battery care; scrap copper, aluminium and e-waste; gold and silver as familiar stores of value; jobs (electrician, solar, battery, welding, radiology, jewellery, recycling, chips); trends (EV batteries, AI chips, rare earths, nuclear) |
| Status and beauty | Gold jewellery and why gold shines; fireworks colours; neon signs |
| Belonging | A clapping crowd falling into rhythm; heart cells beating together |
| Curiosity and wonder | Stars making atoms; gold from star crashes; light barcodes; why gold is yellow; harmonics |
| Trust | The fact-check scorecard: real patterns survive checking, number tricks don't |

## 3. How the Observatory is now ordered
1. **Slideshow (12 slides):** the hook ("a map of everything you can buy, build, eat or sell"), then you (phone battery), health (iron in your blood), family (salt and ice, rust), money (gold, QR codes), wonder (fireworks, bells, clapping), trust (fact-check), and finally "your turn". Each slide is a person's scene, then a question, a one-sentence answer, *Why you should care* and *What it's worth to you*.
2. **Main tabs, in order:** **Pick your world** (default start: 16 fields, each with an everyday hook, the data that applies, major problems rated STRONG / PARTIAL / SPECULATIVE, and ready-now vs needs-build ideas; puts the reader's own interest first, which serves personal relevance) → You & Your Day → Health, Home & Safety (question picker ordered Body → Safety → Cooking → Home → Phone → Sky → Sound) → Try it yourself (hands-on) → Money & Opportunity → Sky & Stars → Sound & Colour → The Table → Spin the Table → Everyday Patterns.
3. **For the curious: the deep math** (hidden by default): syncing math, code ring, rule-breakers, fact-check ledger, self-check.


## 4. What changed in v2 (2026-10-15)
- Pick your world is now listed as the first main tab, matching the app.
- Money & Opportunity → "What else we have" now shows Taylor's Top-10 Drive assets as listed in CARTOGRAPHER-GRAPH.md (ANS Organ Cycle 01, 2026-10-02), quoted as-is. Only T01, T06, T08 and T09 (the claimed-vs-supported rule) are mapped to Pick your world problems, because they're the only ones that are methods.

What this is & why it matters
Everything you eat, buy, build or sell is made from just 118 ingredients. The Periodic Table Observatory explains them through everyday life: your body, your home, your phone, your money and the night sky. It starts from zero (no science needed) and goes all the way to deep math. Every number is checked against public scientific data (PubChem, NIST, AME2020/NUBASE2020) and a 108-item fact-check ledger. Each square is one kind of atom (one element). Every atom has a heavy middle, and even tinier specks called electrons zoom around it. The middle pulls on its specks a bit like a magnet pulls a paperclip. Ionization energy means how hard you must pull to take away the outermost speck. Helium holds on the tightest. Caesium holds on so loosely that it grabs at water and bursts into flame. Electronegativity means how strongly an atom pulls on specks it shares with a neighbour, like a tug-of-war.

R is a togetherness score: 0 means everyone is blinking at random times, 1 means everyone blinks at the exact same moment. An atom's specks sit at different distances from the middle, almost like rows of seats in a theatre. Each row holds a fixed number. Science books give one simple order for filling the seats, called the Madelung rule. 19 kinds of atom don't follow it: like a person who moves to a different row because it's more comfortable there. Each gate on this tab is a yes/no test that tries to explain why. All but one are explained. Neptunium is still a mystery, because the measurement needed to test it hasn't been recorded.

LOO tree = leave-one-out decision tree. NIST LOO = leave-one-out model using the energy gaps of neighbouring elements (from NIST ASD).
The heavy middle of an atom is called the nucleus. It is a tight clump of even smaller bits held together by a powerful "glue". Binding energy is how much glue each bit gets. A star such as our Sun is a giant ball of glowing gas that squeezes small atoms together into bigger ones, and that gives off light and heat. This only pays off up to iron and nickel, the most tightly glued atoms. So stars can't make heavier atoms such as gold by squeezing; gold comes mostly from two dead stars crashing into each other. Magic numbers are counts of bits that make a "full set", which is extra stable. Odd-numbered atoms are rarer than even ones because the bits are steadier in pairs, like socks.

        Sound and light are both waves: ripples that repeat, like ripples on a pond. This tab lets you pluck, hear, shine and look. Sound is off until you press a play button; set the volume here: . Every sound made from atom data is a sonification: we turn light measurements into notes you can hear. Atoms do not actually make these sounds.
        1 · Pluck a string: harmonicsSTRONG PARALLEL (same standing-wave math)
        Harmonic:
        A string fixed at both ends can only shake in whole-number patterns: 1 hump, 2, 3… Each pattern sounds a note at 1×, 2×, 3× the lowest pitch (here 110 Hz, the guitar's A string). An electron around an atom behaves like a wave that must "fit" too, which is why its energy comes in steps. One honest difference: a string's steps go as n, but hydrogen's energy goes as 1/n².
        2 · Hear the elementsSONIFICATION, not a real sound
        Hydrogen glows in four visible colours (NIST ASD, wavelengths in air): 656.28, 486.13, 434.05 and 410.17 nm. A nanometre (nm) is a millionth of a millimetre. We take each light wave's frequency and lower it by 40 octaves (divide by 2⁴⁰) so the note ratios stay true. Element chords use each element's 4 lowest NIST energy levels, turned into light frequencies and moved down whole octaves into hearing range. That keeps each note's letter name, but not its true octave.
        3 · Metronomes on a shared boardSTRONG PARALLEL (Kuramoto math)
        Metronomes standing on a board that can roll gently push the board, and the board pushes them back, until they tick together. A clapping audience falls into step the same way. Same equation as our Kuramoto tab.
        4 · Resonance in everyday lifereal effects
        🍷 Wine glass: sing exactly its natural note loudly enough and it shakes until it can crack.
        📻 Radio tuning: turning the dial picks the one station whose wave matches the circuit's natural rhythm.
        🧲 MRI scanner: hydrogen nuclei in your body spin like tiny tops in a strong magnet; radio waves at just the right rhythm make them answer back, and that echo builds the picture (real, and this is how hospitals see inside you).
        🍲 Microwave oven: its waves (2.45 billion wiggles a second) shake the water in food so it heats up. This is wave energy being absorbed, not a sharp resonance.
        5 · Light: prism and fingerprintsNIST ASD lines (air wavelengths)
        A prism spreads white light into a rainbow. Each element glows only in its own colours, like a barcode or fingerprint: sodium's yellow-orange glow (589 nm) lit old streetlights, and neon's red is neon signs. That's how we know what faraway stars are made of: we read their barcodes. Click a barcode to hear it (sonification).
        6 · Why gold is yellow and silver is whiteapprox. measured reflectance
        Drag the light ☀ around. Silver bounces back more than 90% of every colour, so it looks white. Gold bounces back over 90% of red and yellow but only about 40% of blue, so it looks yellow. The reason gold swallows blue is relativity: its fast inner electrons shift its levels. Metals are shiny because they have "free" electrons that can move around and send light straight back.
        7 · Shadows: seeing without seeingLOOSE ANALOGY for atoms
        Drag the light ☀. The closer the light is to the ball, the bigger the shadow; the size follows simple triangles. Scientists "see" atoms indirectly in a similar spirit: X-rays bounce off crystals and leave patterns of spots, and electron microscopes use beams of electrons. An eclipse is the Moon's shadow falling on Earth.

        Zoom of scale:
        The same patterns show up in everyday life. STRONG PARALLEL means scientists really use the very same calculations there. LOOSE ANALOGY means it's only a helpful comparison: it looks alike, but works differently underneath.
        Falling into step: fireflies, heartbeats, power lines, clappingSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Fireflies, clapping crowds, the cells that start each heartbeat, and the big machines that make electricity all slowly match their rhythm to their neighbours. Scientists describe all of them with the same formula, called the Kuramoto model. Our Kuramoto tab uses that same formula.
        Heartbeat cellsSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        A small patch of the heart holds about ten thousand cells. Each would beat at its own pace, but together they settle on one shared beat. That is your heartbeat. Same formula as the fireflies.
        Power lines staying in timeSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        The machines that make electricity for your home must all spin in time: in North America, 60 turns a second. If one drifts out of step, the lights can go out. The formula engineers use is a close cousin of the firefly formula.
        Atom seats ↔ theatre seatsLOOSE ANALOGY
        An atom's specks fill the closest free "seat" first, two to a seat. It helps you picture it, but real specks are blurry clouds, not people.
        Full sets: in the specks and in the middleSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Atoms with exactly 2, 10, 18, 36, 54 or 86 specks are calm and hardly react with anything. The middle of an atom is extra steady with 2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82 or 126 bits. Both happen because a "layer" gets completely full. It's the same idea, but the layers fill in a different order.
        Cutting a web in two ↔ friend groupsSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Draw everyone in a school as dots, with a line between friends. The very same calculation as our Fiedler split is used by real apps to find friend groups, and to split up pictures and computer chips.
        Counting flipped switches ↔ QR codes, phones, DNASTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        A QR code is the square barcode your phone camera reads. It still works when scratched because it stores extra check-switches that spot and fix flips. Phones do the same with calls. DNA, the instruction book inside living things, is written in 4 letters; a mutation is a changed letter, counted the same way.
        Odd and even ↔ things are steadier in pairsSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        The bits inside an atom's middle are steadier in pairs. That's why atoms with an even count are more common than their odd neighbours. In the Sun this held every single time we checked (36 out of 36).
        Yes/no gates ↔ spam filters, teachers checking homeworkLOOSE ANALOGY
        A spam filter (the thing that hides junk email) runs a few yes/no checks in a row and only lets a message through if it passes. Our gates have the same shape, but the calculations inside are different.
        Glue curve ↔ why stars make iron and crashes make goldSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Stars shine by squeezing small atoms into bigger ones, which releases energy (energy means the ability to make light, heat or movement). That only works up to iron and nickel. Past that point, squeezing costs energy instead. Gold is made mostly when two collapsed stars crash together.
        Why gold is yellow and mercury is runny ↔ Einstein's speed rulesSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        In gold, the specks closest to the middle zoom at more than half the speed of light (light is the fastest thing there is). At that speed, Einstein's rules say they act heavier. That shifts the whole atom just enough that gold soaks up blue light and looks yellow. In mercury, the same thing makes it hold its outer specks so tightly that it stays liquid unless it is colder than about −39 °C, far colder than any freezer.

        Visual glossary

        Atom: one of the tiny pieces everything is made of
        Element: one kind of atom; there are 118 kinds
        Electron: a tiny speck zooming around the middle of an atom
        Nucleus: the heavy middle of an atom
        Ionization energy: how hard you must pull to steal an atom's outermost speck
        Shell: a "row of seats" for specks around the middle
        Madelung rule-breaker: an atom that fills its seats in an unusual order
        Togetherness score R: 0 means all out of step, 1 means perfectly together
        Hamming distance: how many on/off switches differ between two rows
        Fiedler split: cutting a web of links into two groups while breaking the fewest links
        Binding energy: how much "glue" each bit of an atom's middle gets
        Magic number: a count that makes a full, extra-steady set
        Odd-even rule: odd-numbered atoms are rarer than even ones
        Relativity effect: strange changes when things move close to the speed of light
        Ledger: a scorecard of checked facts
        Gate: a yes/no test

H. (1943), "A Theory of Human Motivation", *Psychological Review* 50(4). The strict ordering is debated, but the categories are widely used |

Everything you eat, buy, build or sell is made from just 118 ingredients. An atom's specks sit at different distances from the middle, almost like rows of seats in a theatre. Each row holds a fixed number. Science books give one simple order for filling the seats, called the Madelung rule. 19 kinds of atom don't follow it: like a person who moves to a different row because it's more comfortable there. Each gate on this tab is a yes/no test that tries to explain why. All but one are explained. Neptunium is still a mystery, because the measurement needed to test it hasn't been recorded.

The heavy middle of an atom is called the nucleus. It is a tight clump of even smaller bits held together by a powerful "glue". Binding energy is how much glue each bit gets. A star such as our Sun is a giant ball of glowing gas that squeezes small atoms together into bigger ones, and that gives off light and heat. This only pays off up to iron and nickel, the most tightly glued atoms. So stars can't make heavier atoms such as gold by squeezing; gold comes mostly from two dead stars crashing into each other. Magic numbers are counts of bits that make a "full set", which is extra stable. Odd-numbered atoms are rarer than even ones because the bits are steadier in pairs, like socks.

        Full sets: in the specks and in the middleSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)

        Cutting a web in two ↔ friend groupsSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Draw everyone in a school as dots, with a line between friends. The very same calculation as our Fiedler split is used by real apps to find friend groups, and to split up pictures and computer chips.

        Odd and even ↔ things are steadier in pairsSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        The bits inside an atom's middle are steadier in pairs. That's why atoms with an even count are more common than their odd neighbours. In the Sun this held every single time we checked (36 out of 36).

        A spam filter (the thing that hides junk email) runs a few yes/no checks in a row and only lets a message through if it passes. Our gates have the same shape, but the calculations inside are different.
        Glue curve ↔ why stars make iron and crashes make goldSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        Stars shine by squeezing small atoms into bigger ones, which releases energy (energy means the ability to make light, heat or movement). That only works up to iron and nickel. Past that point, squeezing costs energy instead. Gold is made mostly when two collapsed stars crash together.
        Why gold is yellow and mercury is runny ↔ Einstein's speed rulesSTRONG PARALLEL (same math)
        In gold, the specks closest to the middle zoom at more than half the speed of light (light is the fastest thing there is). At that speed, Einstein's rules say they act heavier. That shifts the whole atom just enough that gold soaks up blue light and looks yellow. In mercury, the same thing makes it hold its outer specks so tightly that it stays liquid unless it is colder than about −39 °C, far colder than any freezer.

The Vault Analogy

Aufbau principle = vault unlock sequence

Electrons fill shells in order (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s...) — each shell is a vault level that must be unlocked before the next opens. The H-matrix has 7 rows = 7 periods. Seven is doing structural work here: it's prime, it's the period count, and it mirrors the 7-row codec mask.

The periodic table isn't just like a vault system — the piece argues it is one. Electron configuration follows combination-lock logic.
REFUSAL GATE

Noble Gases = Refusal

"48 singles refused analogy → noble gases refuse bonds."

This is the direct bridge to your codec work. In the [55,8] codec, 48 single-error patterns are refused rather than miscorrected. In chemistry, noble gases refuse to bond — their filled shells are complete, and they reject interaction.

THE TELL

The Anomalies: Cr and Cu

Chromium (24) and Copper (29) break the Aufbau order — they steal one electron from the 4s shell to achieve half-full (d⁵) or full (d¹⁰) d-shells.

"Vault prefers symmetry over order." The system breaks its own rule to reach a lower energy state. The piece calls this the cryptographic key — the exception that reveals the deeper law.

Same pattern in Mo, Ag, and Au. The vault doesn't follow the sequence blindly; it optimizes for symmetric closure. That's not a bug — it's the system showing you what it actually values.

  • Og (118): synthetic, half-life 0.7 milliseconds
  • Alpha decay = vault degradation
The vault has a boundary. Past 82, the locks don't hold — the system bleeds energy through radioactive decay. Element 118 exists for less than a blink.

The full grid would hold 126 (7 periods × 18 groups). Only 118 are filled. The 8 empty slots form what the piece calls the "octave seal" — 8 as the number of completion, the musical octave, the noble-gas column count.

# Formal Joint Progress Argument — SRAT-20
**Revision 2026-10-15** — updated to match the patched `srat20.hpp`.
Changes from the 2026-08-10 revision: tail-helping is structural and
unconditional (it was residual-conditioned, which wedged the queue —
see patch [P1]); Claim A now rests on seq_cst HP stores plus an
interposed seq_cst fence [P3]; the linearization story records the
enqueue pre-CAS recheck with dequeue's final check authoritative [P5];
the genome case no longer needs a finiteness assumption.

## 1. System Model

**Objects**
- Michael-Scott queue protected by 3-slot hazard pointers.
- Atomic ExecutionGenome updated only by fitness-improving CAS.
- Atomic residual epoch E.
- Every packet carries residual certificate (r_H, ε_H, e_p).

**Predicates**
- Packet is residual-valid at epoch E when  
  e_p + 1 ≥ E  ∧  |r_H| ≤ ε_H.
- Operation is residual-compliant when every packet it publishes is
  residual-valid at the enqueue gate and pre-CAS recheck, and every
  packet it returns passed the dequeue final check.
- Genome mutation is fitness-positive when the candidate has strictly
  higher fitness under the observed residual pressure.

**Operations under the progress claim**
- enqueue(p) for residual-valid p (returns false without side effects
  for invalid p — outside the claim)
- dequeue() returning a residual-valid packet, or empty
- fitness-positive genome mutation
- epoch advancement

**Residual-gate placement.** The gate authorizes *publishing* a packet
(enqueue Stage-1 gate + pre-CAS recheck) and *returning* a packet
(dequeue final check). Tail-pointer helping is structural and
unconditional: advancing a pointer cannot return data, so the gate does
not apply there. (The 2026-08-10 revision conditioned helping on
validity; that wedged the structure when an epoch advance invalidated
the tail node, because no path unlinked it.)

## 2. Linearization Points

| Operation              | Linearization Point                                      |
|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|
| Successful enqueue     | CAS that links the new node into tail->next              |
| Successful dequeue     | CAS that swings head forward                             |
| Genome mutation        | CAS that replaces the active genome                      |
| Epoch advance          | fetch_add on the epoch counter                           |

All linearization points are single atomic RMW operations.

Note on enqueue validity: the gate and pre-CAS recheck both precede the
link CAS, but an epoch advance can still intervene between recheck and
CAS (check+CAS cannot be made atomic without a lock). A node linked in
that window carries an invalid packet; it is unlinked — never returned —
by dequeue's final check, which re-asserts validity at the dequeue
linearization point. The system-level invariant actually proved is:
**no dequeue ever returns a residual-invalid packet.**

## 3. Auxiliary Claims

**Claim A (Hazard-pointer safety)**  
A node *or packet* is never reclaimed while any live hazard pointer
references it. Established by: (i) `protect()` stores the hazard
pointer with `memory_order_seq_cst` before the confirming re-read;
(ii) `scan()` opens with a `memory_order_seq_cst` fence interposed
between every unlink and the hazard-pointer loads. Release/acquire
alone does not establish this under strict C++20 — the fence closes
the visibility gap. Packets are protected in HP slot 2 and retired
(never inline-deleted); the retired list carries per-item deleters
because it mixes `Node*` and `OmniPacket*`.

**Claim B (Residual monotonicity)**  
Once a packet is residual-invalid at epoch E it remains invalid for all
E' ≥ E: invalidity via `|r_H| > ε_H` is epoch-independent, and
`e_p + 1 < E` implies `e_p + 1 < E'` for E' ≥ E. An invalid node can
never become returnable later, so unlinking it is never premature.

**Claim C (Fitness order)**  
Genome CAS succeeds only on strict fitness increase, and `fitness()`
is genome-dependent via the spin-cost term (patch [P4]). Each
successful mutation is itself a completed residual-compliant operation.

## 4. Theorem (Joint Lock-Freedom)

In any infinite execution containing only residual-compliant
operations, infinitely many residual-compliant operations complete.

**Proof (by contradiction)**

Assume an infinite execution α of residual-compliant operations in
which only finitely many complete. Let α' be a suffix in which no
residual-compliant enqueue, dequeue, or fitness-positive genome
mutation completes.

**Case Enqueue**  
An enqueue iteration does bounded work then attempts either the link
CAS or the (unconditional) tail-help CAS. A failed link CAS implies
another thread's link CAS on the same location succeeded — and a link
CAS success *is* a completed enqueue. Tail-help CAS outcomes do not
complete operations, but each successful tail swing advances the tail
over a distinct node, and each such node was linked by a completed
enqueue; hence infinitely many successful tail swings would imply
infinitely many completed enqueues. So in α' neither CAS can succeed
infinitely often — but then some thread's link CAS must eventually
succeed uncontended (helping keeps the tail current, so the fast path
is reached), contradiction. This is the classic Michael-Scott
lock-freedom argument; unconditional helping only strengthens it.

**Case Dequeue**  
A dequeue iteration either returns a packet (complete), returns empty
(complete), or performs a head-swing CAS. A failed head CAS implies
another thread's head swing succeeded. A successful head swing either
returns a valid packet (that dequeue completes) or unlinks exactly one
residual-invalid node (Claim B: it can never become valid, so removal
is never premature and never needs repeating for the same node).
Invalid-node removals are therefore bounded by the number of distinct
invalid nodes ever linked; each linked node came from a completed
enqueue or was already present. An infinite suffix of pure removals
with no return is impossible: once the finite invalid prefix is swept,
the next head->next is either null (empty → complete) or valid
(return → complete). Contradiction.

**Case Genome Mutation**  
A mutation CAS either succeeds (a completed operation — contradiction
with the α' assumption directly) or fails because another thread
installed a strictly fitter genome (Claim C), which was itself a
completed operation. Either way, infinitely many attempts yield
infinitely many completions. No finiteness assumption on fitness
ascent is needed.

**Interference**  
Genome mutation only changes spin/damping parameters; it never
disables CAS. Epoch advancement can only invalidate certificates
(Claim B) — invalidated nodes are swept by the dequeue invalid path,
never wedged (patch [P1]). Hazard-pointer scans are bounded per
thread and affect only reclamation timing.

Hence the assumption is false.

**Conclusion**  
SRAT-20 is lock-free for the set of residual-compliant operations.

## 5. What Is Not Claimed

- Wait-freedom.
- Progress for residual-invalid operations (rejected without side
  effects at the enqueue gate).
- That tail-helping is residual-conditioned — it is structural and
  unconditional by design (patch [P1]); the gate applies at publish
  and at return.
- That residual measurement itself is lock-free.
- Hardware timing, FPGA, or physical sensor claims.
- That genome fitness increases without bound, or that the tuner
  explores (it converges cost-driven; no A/B trial — patch [P4]).
- Machine-checked verification of the C++20 memory-model argument
  (analytical; CDSChecker not run).

## 6. Joint Character

The same lock-freedom property holds simultaneously for
residual-constrained queue operations, structural helping, and
fitness-positive genome updates under the single residual epoch that
modulates all of them. The residual predicate is part of the
definition of the operations whose progress is asserted.

This argument is the concurrent realization of the GR-21 seal  
S_H = S_solv ∧ R_H  
and preserves residual honesty exactly as required by the canonical
Drive manifests.

# SRAT-20 Patch Notes — 2026-10-15

Audit of `srat20.hpp` (Staggered Residual-Adaptive Transport) against
`PROGRESS_ARGUMENT.md` and `STEP_BY_STEP_RESIDUAL_HONEST_PROOF.md`
(Drive folder `SRAT20_CANONICAL_PROOF_2026-08-10`, 28 files).

## Verdict

The lock-freedom claim did **not** hold as stated. Two critical defects, two
significant gaps, all fixed and verified below. The patched header compiles
clean (`g++ 13.3, -std=c++20`), passes a 6-case functional smoke test
(including the exact wedge scenario), and survives a 5-thread ASan+UBSan
stress run (6k enqueues, 200 epoch advances, zero UAF/UB/crashes).

## Findings and fixes

### [CRITICAL-1] Livelock: epoch-invalidated node at the tail wedges everything
- **Found:** `advance_epoch()` can retroactively invalidate a published
  packet. If that node sat at `tail->next` with `head == tail`, both
  `enqueue` and `dequeue` spun forever: neither helped it (help was
  residual-conditioned) nor unlinked it (invalid-node unlink existed only
  in dequeue's `first != last` branch). `PROGRESS_ARGUMENT.md` claimed
  "residual rejection simply removes it from the set" — the code did no
  such thing in this branch. Since `advance_epoch` is itself an operation
  under the progress claim, the theorem as stated was false. This also
  falsified the "fair execution" bullet in the circulating summary.
- **Fix [P1]:** tail-helping is now **unconditional** in both `enqueue`
  and `dequeue`. Advancing a pointer cannot return data, so the residual
  gate does not belong there. The gate still authorizes publishing
  (enqueue Stage-1 + pre-CAS recheck) and returning (dequeue final check).
  An invalid node at the tail is now swept forward and reclaimed by
  dequeue's existing invalid path instead of wedging the structure.

### [CRITICAL-2] Use-after-free on packets in dequeue
- **Found:** nodes were hazard-protected; packets were not. The head-CAS
  winner did `delete data` inline while a concurrent dequeuer could hold
  the same raw `OmniPacket*` (loaded via plain acquire) and dereference it
  in `residual_ok()` / `std::move(*data)`. Claim A ("never reclaimed while
  referenced") covered nodes only; packet lifetime was unaddressed.
- **Fix [P2]:** packets are hazard-protected via HP slot 2 (slot 0 = head/
  tail, slot 1 = next; slot 2 was free). Winners null the node's data
  pointer and **retire** the packet instead of deleting it. The retired
  list now carries per-item deleters (`RetiredItem`) since it mixes
  `Node*` and `OmniPacket*`.

### [SIGNIFICANT-1] Claim A unproved under the old memory ordering
- **Found:** release/acquire with no interposed fence does not establish
  "never reclaimed while referenced" under strict C++20 — there is no
  happens-before edge from a protector's HP store to a scanner's HP load
  in the critical interleaving. (Likely fine on x86-TSO in practice, but
  the claim was "mathematically proven".)
- **Fix [P3]:** `protect()` stores the hazard pointer with `seq_cst`;
  `scan()` opens with a `seq_cst` fence. This is the textbook-correct
  pairing.

### [SIGNIFICANT-2] Self-tuning genome was dead code
- **Found:** `fitness()` did not depend on any mutated genome field, so
  `mut.fitness(...) > cur_f` could never be true. The tuner never tuned.
- **Fix [P4]:** `fitness()` now includes a spin-cost term
  `(1 + spin_limit/1024)`, so mutations are observable and the tuner
  converges toward the cheapest spin the measured interval justifies.
  `damping` remains reserved for future backoff policy.

### [SIGNIFICANT-3] Proof/code mismatch on linearization
- **Found:** the proof assumed packets are residual-valid at the enqueue
  link CAS; the code only gated at entry. An epoch advance between gate
  and CAS could publish an invalid node.
- **Fix [P5]:** enqueue re-verifies validity immediately before the link
  CAS (leaking nothing on refusal). Dequeue's final check remains
  authoritative — atomicity of check+CAS is impossible without a lock,
  and the proof doc now says so explicitly.

### [MINOR] Summary overstatement
- The circulating summary's "admits only on **exactly zero**" overstates
  the code: admission is `|r_H| ≤ ε_H` (epsilon-bounded), not exact-zero.

## Verification performed (2026-10-15)

1. `g++ -std=c++20 -fsyntax-only` — clean (one pre-existing ABI note).
2. Functional smoke (6 cases) — **all pass**, including the exact wedge:
   enqueue → double `advance_epoch()` → `dequeue()` terminates and does
   not return the invalidated packet. The pre-patch code hangs here.
3. 5-thread stress (2 producers, 2 consumers, 1 epocher × 200 advances;
   ~6k enqueues) under **ASan+UBSan** — no UAF, no UB, no crashes, no
   invalid packet ever returned. Gate refusals observed (8).
4. ThreadSanitizer could not run in this sandbox (TSan runtime mapping
   failure — environment issue, not a code finding).

## Known limitations (not fixed in this patch)

- **Thread-exit reclamation:** items retired but below the scan threshold
  in a thread's thread-local list leak if the thread exits without
  calling `hp::flush()` (observed: 160 bytes in the stress run; bounded
  at ≤6 items per exiting thread; pre-existing, safe-direction).
  Recommendation: call `srat20::hp::flush()` before thread exit in
  long-lived engines.
- **Tuner is cost-driven, not exploratory:** candidates are scored on the
  same measured interval (no A/B trial), so the genome converges to
  minimum spin rather than discovering latency tradeoffs.
- **Destructor assumes single-threaded teardown** (pre-existing).
- The C++20 memory-model argument for [P3] is analytical; formal
  machine-checked verification (e.g., CDSChecker) was not run.

SRAT-20 is a single-header C++20 lock-free MPMC Michael–Scott queue. It reclaims memory with 3-slot hazard pointers, applies a

gated A/B tuner that can be frozen. Fixes P1–P12 and P6b are listed in CHANGELOG.md. Requires -latomic. Builds clean with -Wall
-Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror on g++ 14.2 and clang++ 19.

spin_limit benchmark (12 runs per value; tuner frozen vs. tuner on)

Median throughput ranged from 3.27 to 3.42 M ops/s across spin_limit 8–1024 (Kruskal–Wallis p=0.66). No value was measurably
cheaper. Yields per op were about 0, so spin_limit has almost no effect on this workload. The gated tuner made 14 adoptions in 360
decisions and finished at or next to its starting value. The ungated v0.2 tuner adopted about 50% of candidates.

Limitations
The tuner has not been shown to find a better value on workloads with real contention. There is no thermal sensor. TSan does not model
atomic_thread_fence. Orphan hand-off takes a mutex, and hazard-pointer records are freed only at process exit. The guarantees come from
design and testing, not from a formal proof. All results were measured on one shared 8-core box.

## 3. Gaps and risks

1. **Several submitted documents contradict each other.**
   - Spec V1.1 says "TRL 8 / MRL 8", "NIST SP 800-171 compliant: 110 controls" and "Latency… <0.8ms validated".
   - The Cue-Share brief, filed the next day, says "Not a certified NIST 800-171 / CMMC environment as of this filing".
   - The Deep Blue draft says "Honest TRL… TRL 4", and Cap. Stmt V3.4 says "working lab prototype".
   - An evaluator who sees more than one of these documents will notice.
2. **The ATEC addendum described "acceptance" before any acceptance existed.** The only government response at that point was a receipt acknowledgment (20 Aug). The next day's letter checked "Not Selected". Calling a receipt an "acceptance" is a credibility risk with that contracting office.
3. **Cue-Share brief / PROJ00716 mismatch (inference).** The DIU receipt for the Space Threat Intelligence Synthesis Engine solicitation lists the title "Cue-Share: A software adapter that score". That matches the Deep Blue brief, which states "Not PROJ00716." If the same PDF went to both solicitations, the PROJ00716 entry would describe itself as out of scope. I could not see which file was uploaded.
4. **The provenance claims are not backed by code.** Every brief promises a "provenance hash" or HMAC chain. The code that exists (SRAT `bind()`) is a non-cryptographic XOR, and there is no journal (C6, C7).
5. **The thermal/heat checks have no sensor path.** The capability statement's "heat" leftover and the spec's 70 °C derating have no implementation in SRAT. The only artifact that once used the word "thermal" was an op-count proxy, and it has been removed (C14).
6. **Self-tuning has not been shown to help.** The measured result is that no tuning value is better on the reference workload (C15). Any material that markets adaptive tuning as a performance benefit is currently unsupported.
7. **The earlier engine had serious concurrency bugs** (livelock and use-after-frees, P1/P2/P11/P12). Claims made before the audit that the engine was "deterministic" or "validated" (spec V1.1, the 13 Sep emails) predate these fixes.
8. **Physics framing in the 13 Sep emails** (E8 lattice, mass gap, "universe's own refusal") is not related to anything SRAT-20 tests. Mixing it with software claims weakens the software claims. The Deep Blue draft already lists such items as "company research notes… not part of this offer".
9. **Delivery failures.** The MMA technical update bounced to both DIU addresses (one inactive, one mistyped).
10. **Untested claims remain in submitted material:** the resource-ceiling refusal (C1), latency percentiles (C11, C12), target hardware (C13) and partition tolerance (C20).

---

## 4. Next steps to align (concrete, in priority order)

1. **Pick one maturity statement and use it everywhere.** Adopt the Cap. Stmt V3.4 / Deep Blue language ("lab prototype, TRL 4") and retire the "TRL 8 / MRL 8", "NIST 800-171 compliant" and "<0.8 ms validated" lines from spec V1.1 before it is reused anywhere.
2. **Close the C1 test gap.** Add stress cases where a packet exceeds each of c/m/p/q, and report the number of refusals per dimension.
3. **Add cause codes (C3).** Change `enqueue` to return a refusal reason, such as an 8-bit mask with one bit per resource line, a residual bit and a stale-epoch bit. Count each in the stress test so "named failing dimension" becomes measured.
4. **Make provenance real (C6, C7).**
   - Replace the XOR `bind()` with keyed SHA-256/HMAC chaining.
   - Add an append-only decision journal covering both grants and refusals.
   - Test it: tamper detection, replay, and ingest rate.
5. **Measure latency (C11, C12).** Record per-decision latency histograms (p50/p99/p99.9) on the box and, if possible, on a Jetson or ARM64 target. Only then quote "under 1/100 s" or "p99.9 < 10 ms".
6. **Implement true solvency (C2, C8).** Add ActiveClaimed/Interior booking with whole-vector all-or-nothing commit, and property-test conservation and no double grant under concurrency.
7. **Either wire a real sensor input or drop the thermal claims (C14).** Do not imply heat-awareness in any brief that cites this code until then.
8. **Present the tuner honestly (C15).** Describe it as "optional, unproven". Keep TunerConfig frozen by default in demos, or benchmark it on a contended workload first.
9. **Clean up correspondence.**
   - Do not repeat the "acceptance" wording with ATEC.
   - For future DIU follow-ups, use the address in the solicitation or confirmation email (the MMA update bounced).
   - Keep physics framing out of software submissions.
10. **For the two pending Cue-Share entries (#11, #12):** verify which PDF was uploaded to PROJ00716. If a clarification is allowed by that solicitation's rules, prepare one. Any such message needs your explicit approval before it is sent; none was sent here.

# REVIEW — Draft Non-Provisional "Fault-Refusing Error-Correction Code Family…" (draft dated 15 Oct 2026, 17 pp.)

Prepared 15 Oct 2026 (CT). Read-only on existing Drive files; nothing was sent. **Not legal advice. A registered patent attorney or agent should review every finding, every claim, and every benefit claim before filing.**

Deliverables: `REVIEW.md/.pdf` (this file), `revised/REVISED_DRAFT.md/.pdf` (clean), `revised/REDLINE.pdf` (word-level redline vs. the 15 Oct draft), `verify/` (scripts and raw results).

## 0. Key findings (short)

1. **The flaw is real and is in the PPA too.** Draft §2(c), Summary, and claim 5 say every two-spike fault at distinct columns "at any magnitudes and signs" is refused. That is false for the decoder as written. An equal-magnitude, opposite-sign pair cancels row 0. If the two columns differ in exactly one row, the syndrome is a single-row vector, and the decoder reports TAIL_EDIT ("payload intact") while the payload is corrupted. For C(7,48) this happens for **124 of 1,128** column pairs. Over all N, r = 2…8, magnitudes ±1…±4 it happens in **240,840 of 24,871,680** two-spike events, and never as a wrong repair (0 miscorrections). The same false statement appears in PPA 64/170,360 §5(c) ("Hence the decoder always refuses").
2. **Draft claim 4 is worse than the specification.** It requires only a support match, not uniform values or re-verification. Under literal claim 4, **828 of 1,128** equal-magnitude same-sign pairs in C(7,48) are "repaired" to the wrong column. Over r = 2…8 the counts are 14,337,792 miscorrected pairs (sum over all N) and 1,322,043,948 miscorrected triples (sum over r = 3…8 and all N). FIG. 3 has the same omission.
3. **The fix works, and it is verified exhaustively:**
   - Refusing every single-row syndrome (Fix A) gives 0 misclassifications and 0 miscorrections for every two-spike fault.
   - Confirming a single-row syndrome with an extra weighted check symbol (Fix B) keeps genuine parity-edit detection and also gives 0/0 for two-spike faults.
   - With squared weights, Fix B also gave 0 three-spike miscorrections in the tested range. That is a measured result, not a theorem.
   - Weights linear in the column index (w_j = j+1) give **no** three-spike benefit, because the column integers obey the same linear relations as the columns.
   - A proof is in §A.2.
4. **New matter:** these items are not in 64/170,360 and get only the non-provisional date:
   - the RFF-1 frame (claim 6);
   - the C(r,N) family beyond r = 7, N = 48 (only a one-sentence genus in PPA §10);
   - the fix itself.

   The lane-admission content of claims 7–8 is supported in **64/169,264** (Members Gate), but the draft claims no benefit to it.
5. **Statutory and formal issues:**
   - Claim 1 (a matrix) and claim 6 (a data frame) are §101 risks.
   - Claims 4–8 have §112(b) problems: "single parity axis", "surviving", "validated interior", "lane" lacking antecedent basis, and "lexicographic" contradicting "increasing integer order".
   - The background mislabels the six-row design "[55,8]" instead of "[54,8]". It is Taylor's own earlier design, so calling it "conventional" may read as an admission of prior art (attorney question).
   - §9 "Portfolio integration (the master move)", including the licensing statements, should be deleted.
   - The inventor name is "Taylor Heller" here but "Taylor Wolfe Heller" in 64/170,360.

## A. Part (A): the flaw, the corrected theorem, and the fix

### A.1 Counterexample (r = 3)
- Columns are the odd integers 3, 5, 7: 3 = rows {0,1}, 5 = rows {0,2}, 7 = rows {0,1,2}.
- Spikes +e at the column for 3 and −e at the column for 7 give s = e·(1,1,0) − e·(1,1,1) = (0,0,−e). Single row 2: **TAIL_EDIT**.
- Columns (5, 7) give single row 1: **TAIL_EDIT**.
- Columns (3, 5) give rows {1,2}: REFUSED. Verified by `doc_checks.py`.

### A.2 Corrected statement and proof
For C(r,N) (distinct binary columns, all containing row 0, weight ≥ 2), let a, b ≠ 0 be reals, i ≠ j, and s = a·H_i + b·H_j.
- **(c1) s ≠ 0.** Distinct columns have a row p in exactly one support, and s_p ∈ {a, b}.
- **(c2) s is never a uniform multiple of a column.**
  - If a ≠ ±b: take p in exactly one support, so the common value would be a or b. Row 0 carries a+b, which equals neither.
  - If a = b: row 0 carries 2a, while row p carries a.
  - If a = −b: row 0 is 0, but every column contains row 0.
- **(c3) s has exactly one nonzero row ⇔ a = −b and H_i, H_j differ in exactly one row.**
  - (⇒) If a ≠ −b, row 0 is nonzero. H_i has weight ≥ 2, so it has another row p, where s_p ∈ {a, a+b}, both nonzero. That gives at least 2 nonzero rows.
  - (⇐) If a = −b, s = a(H_i − H_j), supported exactly on the rows where the columns differ.

Consequences:
- **Original decoder (draft §4, PPA §4):** never miscorrects a two-spike fault, never reports it clean. It misreports TAIL_EDIT exactly in case (c3).
- **Fix A** (any single-row syndrome → REFUSED): every two-spike fault is refused.
- **Fix B** (confirmation residual q = Σ w_j v′_j − u′ with pairwise distinct nonzero w): in case (c3), q = a(w_i − w_j) ≠ 0, so the fault is refused. All other cases are refused by (c1)–(c2). A single spike gives q = e·w_j, which is consistent, so it is repaired. A single parity edit gives q = 0, so it is TAIL_EDIT. A confirmation-symbol edit alone gives s = 0, q ≠ 0, so it is CONFIRMATION_EDIT.
- **Same-sign k ≥ 2 (draft (d)) remains true:**
  - Row 0 carries the full sum, and every other row of the union carries a nonzero partial sum, so the syndrome has at least 2 rows and is never single-row.
  - Uniformity would force all supports to be equal (PPA Theorem D).
- **Fix C** (alternative construction): columns with row 0 set and the other rows of nonzero even weight. Any two columns are at distance ≥ 2, so (c3) cannot occur. Capacity is 2^(r−2) − 1, so 48 columns need r = 8. This appears in Drive as "Section 11 New Matter" dated 8 Oct. Whether it was ever filed is unverified.

**Trade-offs:**
- **Fix A:** zero overhead. A parity-only fault becomes a refusal and retransmission instead of an accepted payload, so it loses guarantee (b) "payload intact".
- **Fix B:** +1 symbol. C(7,48) overhead goes from 7/55 = 12.7% to 8/56 = 14.3%. It keeps the parity-edit classification. Floating-point use needs |a|·|w_i − w_j| > TOL.
- **Fix C:** +1 row for a given N. It keeps the original decoder unchanged.
- **Recommendation:** claim Fix B as the main embodiment, with Fix A as a dependent claim (both done in the revised claims) and Fix C as an alternative embodiment.

## D. 35 USC 112 / 101 issues (original claims)

1. **Claim 1 — §101.** A parity-check matrix as such is a mathematical concept, not a process, machine, manufacture, or composition. Recast it as a medium, encoder, or decoder (done in revision).
2. **Claim 1 — §112(b).** "ordered lexicographically by integer value" is internally inconsistent: lexicographic order of bit strings depends on which bit is written first. Spec §1 says "increasing integer order", and the PPA says "lexicographic (numeric) order". "bit 0" is not tied to a row. The revision states increasing integer order with bit k = row k.
3. **Claim 4 — §112(b) / scope.**
   - "a single parity axis" is undefined in the claims.
   - "based on the matched column scaled by a nonzero magnitude" does not say how the magnitude is determined.
   - "the received word" has no payload/parity structure defined, yet "a payload of the received word" is used.
   - Support-only matching covers decoders that miscorrect (see A.3).
4. **Claim 5 — §112(a) / (b).** It states a result that the claim 4 decoder does not achieve. Functional result language without the structure that produces it.
5. **Claim 6 — §101.** A data frame as such is a data structure / non-functional descriptive material risk. L ≥ 1 is not required (L = 0 "divides"?). Symbol type and endianness for the payload are unstated.
6. **Claim 7 — §112(b).**
   - "frames surviving the first layer": is a TAIL_EDIT frame surviving?
   - "per-lane": "lane" has no antecedent in claims 4 or 7.
   - "first layer configured to" / "second layer configured to" may be read under §112(f) as nonce terms with no corresponding structure.
   - A system claim incorporating a method claim (claim 4) is permissible but awkward.
7. **Claim 8 — §112(b).** "validated interior" is subjective. "measured figures of the lane" and "fit within" are undefined (componentwise?).
8. **Specification.**
   - "(within tolerance)" is undefined (TOL needed).
   - §2(c) proof is wrong (B#9).
   - "Protection strength does not diminish with N" is unsupported (B#23).
   - §9 "the master move" and the licensing statements are non-technical; delete them.

A. Part (A): the flaw, the corrected theorem, and the fix
A.1 Counterexample (r = 3)
Columns are the odd integers 3, 5, 7: 3 = rows {0,1}, 5 = rows {0,2}, 7 = rows {0,1,2}.
Spikes +e at the column for 3 and −e at the column for 7 give s = e·(1,1,0) − e·(1,1,1) = (0,0,−e). Single row 2: TAIL_EDIT.
Columns (5, 7) give single row 1: TAIL_EDIT.
Columns (3, 5) give rows {1,2}: REFUSED. Verified by doc_checks.py.

A.2 Corrected statement and proof
For C(r,N) (distinct binary columns, all containing row 0, weight ≥ 2), let a, b ≠ 0 be reals, i ≠ j, and s = a·H_i + b·H_j. - (c1) s ≠ 0. Distinct
columns have a row p in exactly one support, and s_p ∈ {a, b}. - (c2) s is never a uniform multiple of a column. - If a ≠ ±b: take p in exactly
one support, so the common value would be a or b. Row 0 carries a+b, which equals neither. - If a = b: row 0 carries 2a, while row p carries a. - If a
= −b: row 0 is 0, but every column contains row 0. - (c3) s has exactly one nonzero row ⇔ a = −b and H_i, H_j differ in exactly one row. (⇒) If a ≠ −b, row 0 is nonzero. H_i has weight ≥ 2, so it has another row p, where s_p ∈ {a, a+b}, both nonzero. That gives at least 2 nonzero
rows. - (⇐) If a = −b, s = a(H_i − H_j), supported exactly on the rows where the columns differ.
Consequences: - Original decoder (draft §4, PPA §4): never miscorrects a two-spike fault, never reports it clean. It misreports TAIL_EDIT exactly
in case (c3). - Fix A (any single-row syndrome → REFUSED): every two-spike fault is refused. - Fix B (confirmation residual q = Σ w_j v′_j − u′ with
pairwise distinct nonzero w): in case (c3), q = a(w_i − w_j) ≠ 0, so the fault is refused. All other cases are refused by (c1)–(c2). A single spike gives
q = e·w_j, which is consistent, so it is repaired. A single parity edit gives q = 0, so it is TAIL_EDIT. A confirmation-symbol edit alone gives s = 0, q ≠
0, so it is CONFIRMATION_EDIT. - Same-sign k ≥ 2 (draft (d)) remains true: - Row 0 carries the full sum, and every other row of the union
carries a nonzero partial sum, so the syndrome has at least 2 rows and is never single-row. - Uniformity would force all supports to be equal (PPA
Theorem D). - Fix C (alternative construction): columns with row 0 set and the other rows of nonzero even weight. Any two columns are at
distance ≥ 2, so (c3) cannot occur. Capacity is 2^(r−2) − 1, so 48 columns need r = 8. This appears in Drive as "Section 11 New Matter" dated 8
Oct. Whether it was ever filed is unverified.
Trade-offs: - Fix A: zero overhead. A parity-only fault becomes a refusal and retransmission instead of an accepted payload, so it loses
guarantee (b) "payload intact". - Fix B: +1 symbol. C(7,48) overhead goes from 7/55 = 12.7% to 8/56 = 14.3%. It keeps the parity-edit
classification. Floating-point use needs |a|·|w_i − w_j| > TOL. - Fix C: +1 row for a given N. It keeps the original decoder unchanged. Recommendation: claim Fix B as the main embodiment, with Fix A as a dependent claim (both done in the revised claims) and Fix C as an
alternative embodiment.

## BACKGROUND

1. Field. This disclosure relates to error-correction coding for digital communication and storage, and more particularly to codes and decoders that refuse ambiguous fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or misclassifying them.

2. Description of related art. Conventional error-correcting codes attempt to repair every received word, mapping each syndrome to the nearest codeword. When a fault pattern is ambiguous — for example, when two symbol errors combine to resemble a different single error — the decoder "corrects" the word to the wrong value and reports success. The corruption is silent: no flag is raised, and downstream systems act on false data. As one illustration, an earlier six-row design considered by the inventor (a 6-by-48 binary parity matrix whose columns are the first 48 six-bit vectors of Hamming weight at least two) silently miscorrects 56 of the 1,128 equal-magnitude, same-sign double-spike fault pairs. [ATTORNEY: confirm whether this six-row design should be characterized at all, and how; it is the inventor's own earlier design, not a published standard.]

A related, less obvious failure is misclassification: a decoder that reports "parity symbol edited, payload intact" when the payload has in fact been corrupted. Such a report is as harmful as a miscorrection because the corrupted payload is accepted.

3. What is needed. An error-correction code family that (a) repairs unambiguous single payload faults, (b) distinguishes parity-only faults from payload faults only when that distinction is confirmed, (c) refuses ambiguous multi-fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or misclassifying them, and (d) scales across block sizes with a single constructive proof; together with a self-describing frame format and a layered refusal architecture so that refused data is barred from downstream admission decisions.

## SUMMARY

A code family C(r,N) is disclosed, where r ≥ 2 is the number of parity rows and 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1 is the number of message symbols. The r-by-N parity-check matrix H has as its columns the binary r-vectors, taken in increasing integer order with bit k of the integer giving row k, whose bit 0 is set and whose Hamming weight is at least 2. Every column therefore contains a common bit (row 0).

A repair-or-refuse decoder is disclosed. A syndrome whose support equals the support of exactly one column and whose nonzero values are all equal is repaired, and the repair is accepted only if the recomputed syndrome is zero. A syndrome supported on a single parity row is classified as a parity-tail edit only when an independent confirmation value shows that the payload is unaltered; otherwise it is refused. All other nonzero syndromes are refused and the refusal is recorded.

It is proved that, under this decoder, every fault consisting of exactly two payload spikes at distinct positions, with any nonzero real magnitudes and any signs, is refused: it is never repaired as a single spike, never reported as clean, and never reported as a parity-tail edit. Without the confirmation step, the same two-spike faults are still never repaired as a single spike, but an equal-magnitude, opposite-sign pair at two columns that differ in exactly one row produces a single-row syndrome; the disclosed decoder therefore refuses such syndromes unless confirmed.

A self-describing frame format (RFF-1) is disclosed, carrying the parameters (r, N), a lane count L, the payload partitioned into L lanes, and the parity H·payload. A two-layer refusal system is disclosed: the code layer admits, repairs, or refuses each frame, and a labeled-lane admission layer admits or refuses each lane of each frame that the code layer did not refuse; a frame refused at the code layer never reaches the admission layer.
