## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### 1. Construction of C(r,N)

Let r ≥ 2 be an integer (the number of parity rows) and let N satisfy 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1 (the number of message symbols). An integer m in 0 … 2^r − 1 is identified with the binary r-vector whose row k is bit k of m (bit 0 is the least significant bit). The parity-check matrix H is the r-by-N binary matrix whose j-th column (0-indexed) is the j-th such vector, taken in increasing integer order, among those with bit 0 set and Hamming weight at least 2 — equivalently, the odd integers 3, 5, 7, … in increasing order.

The bound on N follows by counting: there are 2^(r−1) binary r-vectors with bit 0 set; excluding the weight-1 vector (bit 0 alone) leaves 2^(r−1) − 1 admissible columns.

Every column of H contains bit 0. Example: C(7,48) is the [55,48] code with 7 parity rows protecting 48 message symbols; its columns are the odd integers 3 through 97.

### 2. Decoder

Given a received word with payload estimate v′ (N real values) and parity estimate t′ (r real values), and, in the confirmed embodiment, a received confirmation symbol u′, the decoder performs:

(i) Compute the syndrome s = H·v′ − t′.
(ii) In the confirmed embodiment, compute the confirmation residual q = Σ_j w_j·v′_j − u′, where w_0 … w_(N−1) are pairwise distinct nonzero weights and the transmitted confirmation symbol is u = Σ_j w_j·v_j.
In a preferred embodiment w_j = (j + 1)^2. The weights are preferably not an affine function of the column integer: because the column vectors are binary with no carries, any relation a·H_i + b·H_j + c·H_k = d·H_l among columns also holds among the column integers, so weights affine in the column integer (for example w_j = j + 1, which equals (m_j − 1)/2 for column integer m_j) give no additional protection against such relations, whereas squared weights do in the tested range (section 4).
(iii) If every component of s is zero (and q is zero), output CLEAN. If s is zero and q is nonzero, output CONFIRMATION_EDIT (the confirmation symbol alone was altered; the payload passes all r parity checks).
(iv) Let supp(s) be the set of rows where s is nonzero. If supp(s) equals the support of exactly one column j, all nonzero components of s equal a common value c, and (in the confirmed embodiment) q = c·w_j, subtract c from v′_j, recompute the syndrome, and output REPAIRED only if the recomputed syndrome is zero; otherwise output REFUSED.
(v) If supp(s) is a single row k: in the confirmed embodiment output TAIL_EDIT (payload intact) only if q = 0, and otherwise output REFUSED; in the unconfirmed embodiment output REFUSED (the parity fault is detected but the payload is not accepted).
(vi) Otherwise output REFUSED, store a refusal record comprising at least the syndrome, and take no corrective action.

"Zero" in a floating-point implementation means magnitude not exceeding a tolerance TOL fixed in advance (for example 1e−9 relative to the largest payload magnitude); the guarantees of section 3 are stated for exact arithmetic and hold in floating point for faults whose magnitudes, and whose pairwise differences of weighted contributions, exceed TOL.

### 3. Guarantees (exact arithmetic)

For every instance C(r,N):

(a) Single payload spike. A spike of nonzero magnitude e at position j yields s = e·H_j and q = e·w_j; the support equals that of column j only (columns are distinct), the values are uniform, and the decoder outputs REPAIRED with the payload restored.

(b) Single parity edit. An edit of magnitude f at parity row k yields s = −f·e_k and q = 0. Every column has weight at least 2, so no column matches; the confirmed decoder outputs TAIL_EDIT and the unconfirmed decoder outputs REFUSED.

(c) Two payload spikes. Let a, b be nonzero reals and i ≠ j. Then s = a·H_i + b·H_j and:
 (c1) s is never zero, since s_p = a or b at any row p in exactly one of the two supports, and such a row exists because the columns are distinct.
 (c2) s never matches a column with uniform values. If a ≠ b and a ≠ −b: pick p in one support only, so the common value would be a (or b); row 0 then carries a + b, which differs from both. If a = b: row 0 carries 2a while a row in exactly one support carries a. If a = −b: row 0 carries 0, but every column contains row 0.
 (c3) s has exactly one nonzero row if and only if a = −b and H_i, H_j differ in exactly one row. Proof: if a ≠ −b, row 0 is nonzero, and any other row p of H_i (which exists, weight ≥ 2) carries a or a + b ≠ 0, so at least two rows are nonzero. If a = −b, s = a·(H_i − H_j), supported exactly on the rows where the columns differ.
 Consequently: with the unconfirmed decoder, every two-spike fault is REFUSED; with the confirmed decoder, in case (c3) q = a·(w_i − w_j) ≠ 0, so the fault is REFUSED; in all other cases (c1)–(c2) give REFUSED. Every two-spike fault is therefore refused by both disclosed decoders. A decoder that outputs TAIL_EDIT for every single-row syndrome without confirmation would misclassify exactly the pairs in (c3); for C(7,48) there are 124 such column pairs.

(d) Same-sign faults. For k ≥ 2 spikes at distinct positions with magnitudes all strictly positive or all strictly negative: row 0 carries the total, every other row of the union of supports carries a nonzero partial sum, so s has at least two nonzero rows and is nonzero; and uniformity would require every row of the union to lie in every faulted column, contradicting distinctness. The fault is REFUSED.

(e) Disclosed boundary. Mixed-sign faults of three or more spikes can produce a syndrome equal to a uniform multiple of a single column (example: +1 at the columns for 11 and 13 and −1 at the column for 9 give the syndrome of column 15). With squared weights, the confirmed decoder refused every three-spike fault in the exhaustively tested range (section 4); this is a measured result for that range, not a proof, and three-or-more-spike mixed-sign faults remain outside the guaranteed fault model.

### 4. Verification

The statements of section 3 were checked by exhaustive enumeration in exact integer arithmetic (scripts ecc_verify.py and doc_checks.py) for r = 2 … 8, every N from 1 to 2^(r−1) − 1, every pair of positions with integer magnitudes in {−4 … 4} \ {0}, and every triple of positions with magnitudes in {−3 … 3} \ {0}. Results (counts summed over every N for each r): two-spike faults, 24,871,680 events in total for r = 2 … 8 — decoder as in the 15 Oct draft: 0 miscorrections and 240,840 misclassifications (single-row syndrome reported as a parity edit); unconfirmed decoder (single-row syndromes refused): 0 and 0; confirmed decoder: 0 and 0. Three-spike faults, 2,449,705,032 events in total — decoder as in the 15 Oct draft: 23,903,280 miscorrections and 276,948 misclassifications; unconfirmed decoder: 23,903,280 and 0; confirmed decoder with w_j = j + 1: 23,903,280 and 276,948; confirmed decoder with w_j = (j + 1)^2: 0 and 0. No fault in either battery produced a zero syndrome. For C(7,48): 48 of 48 single spikes repaired; 7 of 7 parity edits classified; 1,128 of 1,128 equal-magnitude same-sign pairs refused; of 1,128 equal-magnitude opposite-sign pairs, 124 produce a single-row syndrome (refused by both disclosed decoders) and 1,004 produce a multi-row syndrome without row 0 (refused).

### 5. RFF-1 self-describing frame format

A frame comprises, in order:
- magic: 4 bytes, value 0x52464631 (ASCII "RFF1");
- r: 1 byte, the parity-row count, 2 ≤ r;
- N: 2 bytes, unsigned big-endian, the message-symbol count, 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1;
- L: 1 byte, the lane count, 1 ≤ L, where L divides N;
- payload: N IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, where lane l (0-indexed) holds symbols l·N/L through (l+1)·N/L − 1;
- parity: r IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, equal to H·payload;
- in the confirmed embodiment, one further IEEE-754 binary64 value u = Σ_j w_j·payload_j, with w_j = j + 1 unless otherwise signaled.

A receiver parses the header, reconstructs H from (r, N) by the construction of section 1, and decodes the frame per section 2. A header with r, N, or L outside the stated ranges is refused.

### 6. Two-layer refusal system

Layer 1 (code): each received frame is decoded per section 2, yielding CLEAN, REPAIRED, TAIL_EDIT, CONFIRMATION_EDIT, or REFUSED. Frames output as REFUSED are recorded and are not passed to Layer 2. Frames output as REPAIRED are passed with the corrected payload; frames output as CLEAN, TAIL_EDIT, or CONFIRMATION_EDIT are passed with the received payload.

Layer 2 (admission): each frame passed by Layer 1 is partitioned into its L lanes. For each lane, a claimed figure C_i and an interior figure I_i are retained under a label i unique within the lane's record, a label-specific headroom H_i = I_i − C_i is computed, and the lane is admitted only if every required label has a corresponding interior label and H_i ≥ 0 for every required label; otherwise the lane is refused. A surplus at one label or lane is not applied to a deficit at another label or lane. Each admission or refusal is written as a new decision record without overwriting the input records (see U.S. Provisional Application No. 64/169,264, paragraphs [0008]–[0010], [0018]–[0022]).

(a) Even-weight construction: columns with bit 0 set whose remaining bits have nonzero even weight; any two such columns differ in at least two rows, so case (c3) cannot occur and no confirmation symbol is needed; capacity is 2^(r−2) − 1 columns (for 48 columns, r = 8). ### 9. Industrial applicability

The family is applicable to any digital link or storage medium where silent data corruption is costlier than retransmission or erasure: radio links, satellite command links, sensor feeds, and autonomous-system sensor buses, among others.

## ABSTRACT

A fault-refusing error-correction code family C(r,N) is disclosed. Its r-by-N binary parity-check matrix uses as columns the odd integers 3, 5, 7, … in increasing order, read as binary r-vectors, so every column shares row 0 and has weight at least two. A repair-or-refuse decoder repairs a single payload fault only on a unique uniform column match confirmed by syndrome collapse, accepts a single-row syndrome as a parity edit only when an independent confirmation value shows the payload unaltered, and otherwise refuses and records the refusal. Every fault of two payload spikes at distinct positions, of any magnitudes and signs, is refused. BACKGROUND
1. Field. This disclosure relates to error-correction coding for digital communication and storage, and more particularly to codes and
decoders that refuse ambiguous fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or misclassifying them.
2. Description of related art. Conventional error-correcting codes attempt to repair every received word, mapping each syndrome to the
nearest codeword. When a fault pattern is ambiguous — for example, when two symbol errors combine to resemble a different single error
— the decoder "corrects" the word to the wrong value and reports success. The corruption is silent: no flag is raised, and downstream
systems act on false data. As one illustration, an earlier six-row design considered by the inventor (a 6-by-48 binary parity matrix whose
columns are the first 48 six-bit vectors of Hamming weight at least two) silently miscorrects 56 of the 1,128 equal-magnitude, same-sign
double-spike fault pairs. [ATTORNEY: confirm whether this six-row design should be characterized at all, and how; it is the inventor's own
earlier design, not a published standard.]
A related, less obvious failure is misclassification: a decoder that reports "parity symbol edited, payload intact" when the payload has in fact been
corrupted. Such a report is as harmful as a miscorrection because the corrupted payload is accepted.
1. What is needed. An error-correction code family that (a) repairs unambiguous single payload faults, (b) distinguishes parity-only faults
from payload faults only when that distinction is confirmed, (c) refuses ambiguous multi-fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or
misclassifying them, and (d) scales across block sizes with a single constructive proof; together with a self-describing frame format and a
layered refusal architecture so that refused data is barred from downstream admission decisions.

SUMMARY
A code family C(r,N) is disclosed, where r ≥ 2 is the number of parity rows and 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1 is the number of message symbols. The r-byN parity-check matrix H has as its columns the binary r-vectors, taken in increasing integer order with bit k of the integer giving row k, whose bit 0
is set and whose Hamming weight is at least 2. Every column therefore contains a common bit (row 0).
A repair-or-refuse decoder is disclosed. A syndrome whose support equals the support of exactly one column and whose nonzero values are all
equal is repaired, and the repair is accepted only if the recomputed syndrome is zero. A syndrome supported on a single parity row is classified as
a parity-tail edit only when an independent confirmation value shows that the payload is unaltered; otherwise it is refused. All other nonzero
syndromes are refused and the refusal is recorded.
It is proved that, under this decoder, every fault consisting of exactly two payload spikes at distinct positions, with any nonzero real magnitudes
and any signs, is refused: it is never repaired as a single spike, never reported as clean, and never reported as a parity-tail edit. Without the
confirmation step, the same two-spike faults are still never repaired as a single spike, but an equal-magnitude, opposite-sign pair at two columns
that differ in exactly one row produces a single-row syndrome; the disclosed decoder therefore refuses such syndromes unless confirmed.
A self-describing frame format (RFF-1) is disclosed, carrying the parameters (r, N), a lane count L, the payload partitioned into L lanes, and the
parity H·payload. A two-layer refusal system is disclosed: the code layer admits, repairs, or refuses each frame, and a labeled-lane admission layer
admits or refuses each lane of each frame that the code layer did not refuse; a frame refused at the code layer never reaches the admission layer.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
1. Construction of C(r,N)
Let r ≥ 2 be an integer (the number of parity rows) and let N satisfy 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1 (the number of message symbols). An integer m in 0 …
2^r − 1 is identified with the binary r-vector whose row k is bit k of m (bit 0 is the least significant bit). The parity-check matrix H is the r-by-N
binary matrix whose j-th column (0-indexed) is the j-th such vector, taken in increasing integer order, among those with bit 0 set and Hamming
weight at least 2 — equivalently, the odd integers 3, 5, 7, … in increasing order.
The bound on N follows by counting: there are 2^(r−1) binary r-vectors with bit 0 set; excluding the weight-1 vector (bit 0 alone) leaves 2^(r−1)
− 1 admissible columns.

 Every column of H contains bit 0. Example: C(7,48) is the [55,48] code with 7 parity rows protecting 48 message symbols; its columns are the odd
integers 3 through 97.

2. Decoder
Given a received word with payload estimate v′ (N real values) and parity estimate t′ (r real values), and, in the confirmed embodiment, a received
confirmation symbol u′, the decoder performs:
(i) Compute the syndrome s = H·v′ − t′. (ii) In the confirmed embodiment, compute the confirmation residual q = Σ_j w_j·v′j − u′, where w_0 …
w(N−1) are pairwise distinct nonzero weights and the transmitted confirmation symbol is u = Σ_j w_j·v_j. In a preferred embodiment w_j = (j +
1)^2. The weights are preferably not an affine function of the column integer: because the column vectors are binary with no carries, any relation
a·H_i + b·H_j + c·H_k = d·H_l among columns also holds among the column integers, so weights affine in the column integer (for example w_j = j
+ 1, which equals (m_j − 1)/2 for column integer m_j) give no additional protection against such relations, whereas squared weights do in the
tested range (section 4). (iii) If every component of s is zero (and q is zero), output CLEAN. If s is zero and q is nonzero, output
CONFIRMATION_EDIT (the confirmation symbol alone was altered; the payload passes all r parity checks). (iv) Let supp(s) be the set of rows where
s is nonzero. If supp(s) equals the support of exactly one column j, all nonzero components of s equal a common value c, and (in the confirmed
embodiment) q = c·w_j, subtract c from v′_j, recompute the syndrome, and output REPAIRED only if the recomputed syndrome is zero; otherwise
output REFUSED. (v) If supp(s) is a single row k: in the confirmed embodiment output TAIL_EDIT (payload intact) only if q = 0, and otherwise
output REFUSED; in the unconfirmed embodiment output REFUSED (the parity fault is detected but the payload is not accepted). (vi) Otherwise
output REFUSED, store a refusal record comprising at least the syndrome, and take no corrective action.
"Zero" in a floating-point implementation means magnitude not exceeding a tolerance TOL fixed in advance (for example 1e−9 relative to the
largest payload magnitude); the guarantees of section 3 are stated for exact arithmetic and hold in floating point for faults whose magnitudes,
and whose pairwise differences of weighted contributions, exceed TOL.

3. Guarantees (exact arithmetic)
For every instance C(r,N):
(a) Single payload spike. A spike of nonzero magnitude e at position j yields s = e·H_j and q = e·w_j; the support equals that of column j only
(columns are distinct), the values are uniform, and the decoder outputs REPAIRED with the payload restored.
(b) Single parity edit. An edit of magnitude f at parity row k yields s = −f·e_k and q = 0. Every column has weight at least 2, so no column
matches; the confirmed decoder outputs TAIL_EDIT and the unconfirmed decoder outputs REFUSED.
(c) Two payload spikes. Let a, b be nonzero reals and i ≠ j. Then s = a·H_i + b·H_j and: (c1) s is never zero, since s_p = a or b at any row p in
exactly one of the two supports, and such a row exists because the columns are distinct. (c2) s never matches a column with uniform values. If a
≠ b and a ≠ −b: pick p in one support only, so the common value would be a (or b); row 0 then carries a + b, which differs from both. If a = b: row
0 carries 2a while a row in exactly one support carries a. If a = −b: row 0 carries 0, but every column contains row 0. (c3) s has exactly one
nonzero row if and only if a = −b and H_i, H_j differ in exactly one row. Proof: if a ≠ −b, row 0 is nonzero, and any other row p of H_i (which exists,
weight ≥ 2) carries a or a + b ≠ 0, so at least two rows are nonzero. If a = −b, s = a·(H_i − H_j), supported exactly on the rows where the columns
differ. Consequently: with the unconfirmed decoder, every two-spike fault is REFUSED; with the confirmed decoder, in case (c3) q = a·(w_i − w_j) ≠
0, so the fault is REFUSED; in all other cases (c1)–(c2) give REFUSED. Every two-spike fault is therefore refused by both disclosed decoders. A
decoder that outputs TAIL_EDIT for every single-row syndrome without confirmation would misclassify exactly the pairs in (c3); for C(7,48) there
are 124 such column pairs.
(d) Same-sign faults. For k ≥ 2 spikes at distinct positions with magnitudes all strictly positive or all strictly negative: row 0 carries the total, every
other row of the union of supports carries a nonzero partial sum, so s has at least two nonzero rows and is nonzero; and uniformity would require
every row of the union to lie in every faulted column, contradicting distinctness. The fault is REFUSED.
(e) Disclosed boundary. Mixed-sign faults of three or more spikes can produce a syndrome equal to a uniform multiple of a single column
(example: +1 at the columns for 11 and 13 and −1 at the column for 9 give the syndrome of column 15). With squared weights, the confirmed
decoder refused every three-spike fault in the exhaustively tested range (section 4); this is a measured result for that range, not a proof, and
three-or-more-spike mixed-sign faults remain outside the guaranteed fault model.

without row 0 (refused).

5. RFF-1 self-describing frame format
A frame comprises, in order: - magic: 4 bytes, value 0x52464631 (ASCII "RFF1"); - r: 1 byte, the parity-row count, 2 ≤ r; - N: 2 bytes, unsigned bigendian, the message-symbol count, 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1; - L: 1 byte, the lane count, 1 ≤ L, where L divides N; - payload: N IEEE-754 binary64
values, big-endian, where lane l (0-indexed) holds symbols l·N/L through (l+1)·N/L − 1; - parity: r IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, equal to
H·payload; - in the confirmed embodiment, one further IEEE-754 binary64 value u = Σ_j w_j·payload_j, with w_j = j + 1 unless otherwise signaled.
A receiver parses the header, reconstructs H from (r, N) by the construction of section 1, and decodes the frame per section 2. A header with r, N,
or L outside the stated ranges is refused.

6. Two-layer refusal system
Layer 1 (code): each received frame is decoded per section 2, yielding CLEAN, REPAIRED, TAIL_EDIT, CONFIRMATION_EDIT, or REFUSED. Frames
output as REFUSED are recorded and are not passed to Layer 2. Frames output as REPAIRED are passed with the corrected payload; frames output
as CLEAN, TAIL_EDIT, or CONFIRMATION_EDIT are passed with the received payload.
Layer 2 (admission): each frame passed by Layer 1 is partitioned into its L lanes. For each lane, a claimed figure C_i and an interior figure I_i are
retained under a label i unique within the lane's record, a label-specific headroom H_i = I_i − C_i is computed, and the lane is admitted only if
every required label has a corresponding interior label and H_i ≥ 0 for every required label; otherwise the lane is refused. A surplus at one label or

 lane is not applied to a deficit at another label or lane. Each admission or refusal is written as a new decision record without overwriting the input
records (see U.S. Provisional Application No. 64/169,264, paragraphs [0008]–[0010], [0018]–[0022]).

ABSTRACT
A fault-refusing error-correction code family C(r,N) is disclosed. Its r-by-N binary parity-check matrix uses as columns the odd integers 3, 5, 7, … in
increasing order, read as binary r-vectors, so every column shares row 0 and has weight at least two. A repair-or-refuse decoder repairs a single
payload fault only on a unique uniform column match confirmed by syndrome collapse, accepts a single-row syndrome as a parity edit only when
an independent confirmation value shows the payload unaltered, and otherwise refuses and records the refusal. Every fault of two payload spikes
at distinct positions, of any magnitudes and signs, is refused. A self-describing frame format carries the parameters, lanes, payload, and parity,
and a two-layer system bars code-refused frames from per-lane, per-label headroom admission.

2. The common-bit theorem.
For every instance C(r,N) of the family, the following hold, proved by the
common-bit argument:
(a) Every single payload spike, at any nonzero magnitude, is repaired.
The syndrome equals the spike magnitude times the spike column; the column
is identified by support matching and the payload is corrected.
(b) Every single parity-tail edit is detected with the payload intact. A
fault confined to one parity symbol produces a syndrome supported on a
single parity axis, which matches no column support.
(c) Every dual-spike fault at distinct columns, at any magnitudes and
signs, is refused. Proof: the syndrome is a*col_i + b*col_j for nonzero a,
b. Bit 0 of the syndrome equals a + b (both columns have bit 0 set). For
the syndrome to equal c*col_k for some column k and scalar c, the supports
must coincide; but col_i and col_j are distinct vectors sharing bit 0, so
their sum has support strictly larger than any single column support, and
no scalar multiple of a binary column can match it. The decoder therefore
cannot misidentify the fault as a single-column event, and refuses.
(d) Every same-sign multi-spike fault of order 2 or greater is refused, by
the same support argument.
The inventor has verified these properties computationally: 48/48 singles
repaired and 1,128/1,128 dual-spike pairs refused with zero miscorrections
for C(7,48); 100/100 singles and 4,950/4,950 pairs refused with zero
miscorrections for C(8,100); and corresponding batteries for C(6,31),
C(7,63), C(8,127), C(9,255), and C(10,511).

outside the proven fault model. This boundary is disclosed so that the
scope of the guarantee is exact.

A frame comprises, in order:
- magic: 4 bytes, value 0x52464631 (ASCII "RFF1");
- r: 1 byte, the parity-row count; count, 2 ≤ r;
- N: 2 bytes, unsigned big-endian, the message-symbol count; count, 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1;
- L: 1 byte, the lane count, 1 ≤ L, where L divides N;
- payload: N 64-bit floats, IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, where lane l (0-indexed) holds symbols
[l*N/L : (l+1)*N/L]; l·N/L through (l+1)·N/L − 1;
- parity: r 64-bit floats IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, equal to H * payload. H·payload;

 - in the confirmed embodiment, one further IEEE-754 binary64 value u = Σ_j w_j·payload_j, with w_j = j + 1 unless otherwise signaled.

FAULT-REFUSING ERROR-CORRECTION CODE FAMILY WITH COMMON-BIT CONSTRUCTION, CONFIRMED TAIL-EDIT CLASSIFICATION, SELF-DESCRIBING FRAME FORMAT, AND TWO-LAYER REFUSAL SYSTEM
CROSS-REFERENCE TO RELATED APPLICATIONS
[0001]	This application claims the benefit under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) of U.S. Provisional Application No. 64/170,360, filed October 6, 2026, entitled "Fault-Refusing Error-Correction Code with Minimal Seven-Row Binary Parity Matrix," and of U.S. Provisional Application No. 64/169,264, filed October 4, 2026 (Members Gate labeled-figure admission control), each of which is incorporated herein by reference in its entirety. [FILER DECISION: confirm the 64/169,264 benefit claim is wanted; it supports claims 11-12. Every benefit claim must also be entered in the Application Data Sheet.]
[0002]	This application is also related to U.S. Provisional Application No. 64/150,688, filed September 8, 2026 (headroom admission control), which is incorporated herein by reference in its entirety.
BACKGROUND
Field
[0003]	This disclosure relates to error-correction coding for digital communication and storage, and more particularly to codes and decoders that refuse ambiguous fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or misclassifying them.
Description of Related Art
[0004]	Conventional error-correcting codes attempt to repair every received word, mapping each syndrome to the nearest codeword. When a fault pattern is ambiguous, for example when two symbol errors combine to resemble a different single error, the decoder corrects the word to the wrong value and reports success. The corruption is silent: no flag is raised, and downstream systems act on false data.
[0005]	As one illustration, an earlier six-row design considered by the inventor, a 6-by-48 binary parity-check matrix whose columns are the first 48 six-bit vectors, in increasing integer order, having Hamming weight at least two (no row being common to all columns), silently miscorrects 56 of the 1,128 equal-magnitude, same-sign double-spike fault pairs when decoded by matching the syndrome to a uniform multiple of a single column.
[0006]	A related, less obvious failure is misclassification: a decoder that reports "parity symbol edited, payload intact" when the payload has in fact been corrupted. Such a report is as harmful as a miscorrection because the corrupted payload is accepted.
What Is Needed
[0007]	What is needed is an error-correction code family that (a) repairs unambiguous single payload faults, (b) distinguishes parity-only faults from payload faults only when that distinction is confirmed, (c) refuses ambiguous multi-fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or misclassifying them, and (d) scales across block sizes with a single constructive proof; together with a self-describing frame format and a layered refusal architecture so that refused data is barred from downstream admission decisions.
SUMMARY
[0008]	A code family C(r,N) is disclosed, where r ≥ 2 is the number of parity rows and 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1 is the number of message symbols. The r-by-N parity-check matrix H has as its columns the binary r-vectors, taken in increasing integer order with bit k of the integer giving row k, whose bit 0 is set and whose Hamming weight is at least two. Every column therefore contains a common bit (row 0).
[0009]	A repair-or-refuse decoder is disclosed. A syndrome whose support equals the support of exactly one column and whose nonzero values are all equal is repaired, and the repair is accepted only if the recomputed syndrome is zero. A syndrome supported on a single parity row is classified as a parity-tail edit only when an independent confirmation value shows that the payload is unaltered; otherwise it is refused. All other nonzero syndromes are refused and the refusal is recorded.
[0010]	Under this decoder, every fault consisting of exactly two payload spikes at distinct positions, with any nonzero real magnitudes and any signs, is refused: it is never repaired as a single spike, never reported as clean, and never reported as a parity-tail edit. Without the confirmation step or the refusal of unconfirmed single-row syndromes, two-spike faults are still never repaired as a single spike, but an equal-magnitude, opposite-sign pair at two columns that differ in exactly one row produces a single-row syndrome indistinguishable from a parity edit; the disclosed decoder therefore refuses such syndromes unless confirmed.
[0011]	A self-describing frame format (RFF-1) is disclosed, carrying the parameters (r, N), a lane count L, the payload partitioned into L lanes, and the parity H·payload. A two-layer refusal system is disclosed: the code layer admits, repairs, or refuses each frame, and a labeled-lane admission layer admits or refuses each lane of each frame that the code layer did not refuse; a frame refused at the code layer never reaches the admission layer.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
1. Construction of C(r,N)
[0018]	Let r ≥ 2 be an integer (the number of parity rows) and let N satisfy 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1 (the number of message symbols). An integer m in 0 … 2^r − 1 is identified with the binary r-vector whose row k is bit k of m (bit 0 is the least significant bit). The parity-check matrix H (100, FIG. 1) is the r-by-N binary matrix whose j-th column (0-indexed) is the j-th such vector, taken in increasing integer order, among those with bit 0 set and Hamming weight at least two; equivalently, the odd integers 3, 5, 7, … in increasing order.
[0019]	The bound on N follows by counting: there are 2^(r−1) binary r-vectors with bit 0 set; excluding the weight-one vector (bit 0 alone) leaves 2^(r−1) − 1 admissible columns.
[0020]	Every column of H contains bit 0, shown as common-bit row 102 in FIG. 1; rows 1 through r−1 are shown as rows 104 and the columns as columns 106. Example: C(7,48) is the [55,48] code with 7 parity rows protecting 48 message symbols; its columns are the odd integers 3 through 97.
2. Decoder
[0021]	Referring to FIG. 3, given a received word with payload estimate v′ (N real values) and parity estimate t′ (r real values), and, in the confirmed embodiment, a received confirmation symbol u′, the decoder performs the following steps.
[0022]	(i) Step 302: compute the syndrome s = H·v′ − t′.
[0023]	(ii) Step 304: in the confirmed embodiment, compute the confirmation residual q = Σ_j w_j·v′_j − u′, where w_0 … w_(N−1) are pairwise distinct nonzero weights and the transmitted confirmation symbol is u = Σ_j w_j·v_j. In a preferred embodiment w_j = (j + 1)^2. The weights are preferably not an affine function of the column integer: because the column vectors are binary, any relation a·H_i + b·H_j + c·H_k = d·H_l among columns also holds among the column integers, so weights affine in the column integer (for example w_j = j + 1, which equals (m_j − 1)/2 for column integer m_j) give no additional protection against such relations, whereas squared weights did in the tested range (section 4).
[0024]	(iii) Step 306: if every component of s is zero and q is zero, output CLEAN (308). If s is zero and q is nonzero, output CONFIRMATION_EDIT: the confirmation symbol alone was altered and the payload passes all r parity checks.
[0025]	(iv) Step 310: let supp(s) be the set of rows where s is nonzero. If supp(s) equals the support of exactly one column j, all nonzero components of s equal a common value c, and (in the confirmed embodiment) q = c·w_j, subtract c from v′_j, recompute the syndrome, and output REPAIRED (312) only if the recomputed syndrome is zero; otherwise output REFUSED.
[0026]	(v) Step 314: if supp(s) is a single row k, then in the confirmed embodiment (step 316) output TAIL_EDIT (318, payload intact) only if q = 0 and otherwise output REFUSED; in the unconfirmed embodiment output REFUSED, the parity fault being detected but the payload not accepted.
[0027]	(vi) Step 320: otherwise output REFUSED, store a refusal record (322) comprising at least the syndrome, and take no corrective action.
[0028]	"Zero" in a floating-point implementation means magnitude not exceeding a tolerance TOL fixed in advance (for example 1e−9 relative to the largest payload magnitude). The guarantees of section 3 are stated for exact arithmetic and hold in floating point for faults whose magnitudes, and whose differences of weighted contributions, exceed TOL.
3. Guarantees (exact arithmetic)
[0029]	The following hold for every instance C(r,N).
[0030]	(a) Single payload spike. A spike of nonzero magnitude e at position j yields s = e·H_j and q = e·w_j. The support equals that of column j only, because the columns are distinct; the values are uniform; and the decoder outputs REPAIRED with the payload restored.
[0031]	(b) Single parity edit. An edit of magnitude f at parity row k yields s = −f·e_k and q = 0. Every column has weight at least two, so no column matches; the confirmed decoder outputs TAIL_EDIT and the unconfirmed decoder outputs REFUSED.
[0032]	(c) Two payload spikes. Let a and b be nonzero reals, i ≠ j, and s = a·H_i + b·H_j. (c1) s is never zero, since s_p equals a or b at any row p lying in exactly one of the two supports, and such a row exists because the columns are distinct. (c2) s never equals a uniform multiple of a column. If a ≠ b and a ≠ −b, the common value would have to be a or b at a row in exactly one support, while row 0 carries a + b, which differs from both. If a = b, row 0 carries 2a while a row in exactly one support carries a. If a = −b, row 0 carries 0, but every column contains row 0. (c3) s has exactly one nonzero row if and only if a = −b and H_i and H_j differ in exactly one row. If a ≠ −b, row 0 is nonzero and any other row p of H_i, which exists because H_i has weight at least two, carries a or a + b, both nonzero, so at least two rows are nonzero. If a = −b, s = a·(H_i − H_j), supported exactly on the rows where the columns differ.
[0033]	Consequently, with the unconfirmed decoder every two-spike fault is REFUSED; with the confirmed decoder, in case (c3) q = a·(w_i − w_j) ≠ 0, so the fault is REFUSED, and in all other cases (c1) and (c2) give REFUSED. A decoder that instead outputs TAIL_EDIT for every single-row syndrome without confirmation would misclassify exactly the pairs of case (c3); for C(7,48) there are 124 such column pairs out of 1,128.
[0034]	(d) Same-sign faults. For k ≥ 2 spikes at distinct positions with magnitudes all strictly positive or all strictly negative, row 0 carries the total and every other row of the union of supports carries a nonzero partial sum, so s has at least two nonzero rows; uniformity would require every row of the union to lie in every faulted column, contradicting distinctness. The fault is REFUSED. For C(7,48), all 17,296 triples of distinct columns were also checked: no combination of three columns with same-sign nonzero amplitudes equals a multiple of any column.
[0035]	(e) Disclosed boundary. Mixed-sign faults of three or more spikes can produce a syndrome equal to a uniform multiple of a single column. Example: +1 at the columns for 11 and 13 and −1 at the column for 9 give the syndrome of column 15. Such relations are structural. For C(7,48), 13,060 of the 17,296 triples of distinct columns have a bitwise exclusive-or equal to a fourth column, and 7,140 of those triples admit nonzero real amplitudes a1, a2, a3 with a1·H_i + a2·H_j + a3·H_k equal to the fourth column exactly. An exclusive-or triple (i, j, k) admits such amplitudes exactly when one of the three supports lies between the intersection and the union of the other two (for example S_i ∩ S_j ⊆ S_k ⊆ S_i ∪ S_j); this sandwich condition agreed with the real-amplitude test for all 13,060 exclusive-or triples of C(7,48). Without a confirmation value, a fault with such amplitudes would be repaired to the wrong column. With squared weights, the confirmed decoder refused every three-spike fault in the exhaustively tested range of section 4; this is a measured result for that range, not a proof, and mixed-sign faults of three or more spikes remain outside the guaranteed fault model.
4. Verification
[0036]	The statements of section 3 were checked by exhaustive enumeration in exact integer arithmetic for r = 2 … 8, every N from 1 to 2^(r−1) − 1, every pair of positions with integer magnitudes in {−4 … 4} \ {0}, and every triple of positions with magnitudes in {−3 … 3} \ {0}. Counts below are summed over every N for each r.

5. RFF-1 Self-Describing Frame Format
[0040]	Referring to FIG. 4, a frame 400 comprises, in order: a magic field 402 of 4 bytes, value 0x52464631 (ASCII "RFF1"); a field 404 of 1 byte giving the parity-row count r, 2 ≤ r; a field 406 of 2 bytes, unsigned big-endian, giving the message-symbol count N, 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1; a field 408 of 1 byte giving the lane count L, 1 ≤ L, where L divides N; a payload 410 of N IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, where lane l (0-indexed) holds symbols l·N/L through (l+1)·N/L − 1; a parity field 412 of r IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, equal to H·payload; and, in the confirmed embodiment, a confirmation field 414 of one further IEEE-754 binary64 value u = Σ_j w_j·payload_j, with w_j = j + 1 unless otherwise signaled.
[0041]	In a version-2 variant, the magic field is 0xD2464631 (0x52464631 with bit 31 set) and the payload, parity, and confirmation values are IEEE-754 binary32; a receiver implementing only version 1 refuses a frame whose magic field it does not recognize.
[0042]	A receiver parses the header, reconstructs H from (r, N) by the construction of section 1, and decodes the frame per section 2. A header with r, N, or L outside the stated ranges is refused.
6. Two-Layer Refusal System
[0043]	Referring to FIG. 5, in Layer 1 (code layer 502) each received frame from channel 500 is decoded per section 2, yielding CLEAN, REPAIRED, TAIL_EDIT, CONFIRMATION_EDIT, or REFUSED. Frames output as REFUSED are recorded in refusal store 504 and are not passed to Layer 2. Frames output as REPAIRED are passed with the corrected payload; frames output as CLEAN, TAIL_EDIT, or CONFIRMATION_EDIT are passed with the received payload.
[0044]	In Layer 2 (admission layer 506), each frame passed by Layer 1 is partitioned into its L lanes. For each lane, a claimed figure C_i and an interior figure I_i are retained under a label i unique within the lane's record, a label-specific headroom H_i = I_i − C_i is computed, and the lane is admitted (508) only if every required label has a corresponding interior label and H_i ≥ 0 for every required label; otherwise the lane is refused (510). A surplus at one label or lane is not applied to a deficit at another label or lane. Each admission or refusal is written as a new decision record without overwriting the input records (see U.S. Provisional Application No. 64/169,264).

ABSTRACT
A fault-refusing error-correction code family C(r,N) uses an r-by-N binary parity-check matrix whose columns are the odd integers 3, 5, 7, and onward in increasing order, read as binary r-vectors, so every column shares row 0 and has weight at least two. A repair-or-refuse decoder repairs a single payload fault only on a unique uniform column match confirmed by a zero recomputed syndrome, accepts a single-row syndrome as a parity edit only when an independent confirmation value shows the payload unaltered, and otherwise refuses and records the refusal. Every fault of two payload spikes at distinct positions, of any magnitudes and signs, is refused. A self-describing frame format carries the parameters, lanes, payload, and parity, and a two-layer system bars code-refused frames from per-lane headroom admission.

BACKGROUND
Field
[0003] This disclosure relates to error-correction coding for digital communication and storage,
and more particularly to codes and decoders that refuse ambiguous fault patterns instead of
miscorrecting or misclassifying them.
Description of Related Art
[0004] Conventional error-correcting codes attempt to repair every received word, mapping each
syndrome to the nearest codeword. When a fault pattern is ambiguous, for example when two
symbol errors combine to resemble a different single error, the decoder corrects the word to the
wrong value and reports success. The corruption is silent: no flag is raised, and downstream
systems act on false data.
[0005] As one illustration, an earlier six-row design considered by the inventor, a 6-by-48 binary
parity-check matrix whose columns are the first 48 six-bit vectors, in increasing integer order,
having Hamming weight at least two (no row being common to all columns), silently miscorrects

1

 56 of the 1,128 equal-magnitude, same-sign double-spike fault pairs when decoded by matching
the syndrome to a uniform multiple of a single column.
[0006] A related, less obvious failure is misclassification: a decoder that reports "parity symbol
edited, payload intact" when the payload has in fact been corrupted. Such a report is as harmful
as a miscorrection because the corrupted payload is accepted.
What Is Needed
[0007] What is needed is an error-correction code family that (a) repairs unambiguous single
payload faults, (b) distinguishes parity-only faults from payload faults only when that distinction
is confirmed, (c) refuses ambiguous multi-fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or
misclassifying them, and (d) scales across block sizes with a single constructive proof; together
with a self-describing frame format and a layered refusal architecture so that refused data is
barred from downstream admission decisions.
SUMMARY
[0008] A code family C(r,N) is disclosed, where r ≥ 2 is the number of parity rows and 1 ≤ N ≤
2^(r−1) − 1 is the number of message symbols. The r-by-N parity-check matrix H has as its
columns the binary r-vectors, taken in increasing integer order with bit k of the integer giving
row k, whose bit 0 is set and whose Hamming weight is at least two. Every column therefore
contains a common bit (row 0).
[0009] A repair-or-refuse decoder is disclosed. A syndrome whose support equals the support of
exactly one column and whose nonzero values are all equal is repaired, and the repair is accepted
only if the recomputed syndrome is zero. A syndrome supported on a single parity row is
classified as a parity-tail edit only when an independent confirmation value shows that the
payload is unaltered; otherwise it is refused. All other nonzero syndromes are refused and the
refusal is recorded.
[0010] Under this decoder, every fault consisting of exactly two payload spikes at distinct
positions, with any nonzero real magnitudes and any signs, is refused: it is never repaired as a
single spike, never reported as clean, and never reported as a parity-tail edit. Without the
confirmation step or the refusal of unconfirmed single-row syndromes, two-spike faults are still
never repaired as a single spike, but an equal-magnitude, opposite-sign pair at two columns that

2

 differ in exactly one row produces a single-row syndrome indistinguishable from a parity edit;
the disclosed decoder therefore refuses such syndromes unless confirmed.
[0011] A self-describing frame format (RFF-1) is disclosed, carrying the parameters (r, N), a
lane count L, the payload partitioned into L lanes, and the parity H·payload. A two-layer refusal
system is disclosed: the code layer admits, repairs, or refuses each frame, and a labeled-lane
admission layer admits or refuses each lane of each frame that the code layer did not refuse; a
frame refused at the code layer never reaches the admission layer.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
1. Construction of C(r,N)
[0018] Let r ≥ 2 be an integer (the number of parity rows) and let N satisfy 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1
(the number of message symbols). An integer m in 0 … 2^r − 1 is identified with the binary rvector whose row k is bit k of m (bit 0 is the least significant bit). The parity-check matrix H
(100, FIG. 1) is the r-by-N binary matrix whose j-th column (0-indexed) is the j-th such vector,
taken in increasing integer order, among those with bit 0 set and Hamming weight at least two;
equivalently, the odd integers 3, 5, 7, … in increasing order.
[0019] The bound on N follows by counting: there are 2^(r−1) binary r-vectors with bit 0 set;
excluding the weight-one vector (bit 0 alone) leaves 2^(r−1) − 1 admissible columns.

3

 [0020] Every column of H contains bit 0, shown as common-bit row 102 in FIG. 1; rows 1
through r−1 are shown as rows 104 and the columns as columns 106. Example: C(7,48) is the
[55,48] code with 7 parity rows protecting 48 message symbols; its columns are the odd integers
3 through 97.
2. Decoder
[0021] Referring to FIG. 3, given a received word with payload estimate v′ (N real values) and
parity estimate t′ (r real values), and, in the confirmed embodiment, a received confirmation
symbol u′, the decoder performs the following steps.
[0022] (i) Step 302: compute the syndrome s = H·v′ − t′.
[0023] (ii) Step 304: in the confirmed embodiment, compute the confirmation residual q = Σ_j
w_j·v′_j − u′, where w_0 … w_(N−1) are pairwise distinct nonzero weights and the transmitted
confirmation symbol is u = Σ_j w_j·v_j. In a preferred embodiment w_j = (j + 1)^2. The weights
are preferably not an affine function of the column integer: because the column vectors are
binary, any relation a·H_i + b·H_j + c·H_k = d·H_l among columns also holds among the
column integers, so weights affine in the column integer (for example w_j = j + 1, which equals
(m_j − 1)/2 for column integer m_j) give no additional protection against such relations, whereas
squared weights did in the tested range (section 4).
[0024] (iii) Step 306: if every component of s is zero and q is zero, output CLEAN (308). If s is
zero and q is nonzero, output CONFIRMATION_EDIT: the confirmation symbol alone was
altered and the payload passes all r parity checks.
[0025] (iv) Step 310: let supp(s) be the set of rows where s is nonzero. If supp(s) equals the
support of exactly one column j, all nonzero components of s equal a common value c, and (in
the confirmed embodiment) q = c·w_j, subtract c from v′_j, recompute the syndrome, and output
REPAIRED (312) only if the recomputed syndrome is zero; otherwise output REFUSED.
[0026] (v) Step 314: if supp(s) is a single row k, then in the confirmed embodiment (step 316)
output TAIL_EDIT (318, payload intact) only if q = 0 and otherwise output REFUSED; in the
unconfirmed embodiment output REFUSED, the parity fault being detected but the payload not
accepted.

4

 [0027] (vi) Step 320: otherwise output REFUSED, store a refusal record (322) comprising at
least the syndrome, and take no corrective action.
[0028] "Zero" in a floating-point implementation means magnitude not exceeding a tolerance
TOL fixed in advance (for example 1e−9 relative to the largest payload magnitude). The
guarantees of section 3 are stated for exact arithmetic and hold in floating point for faults whose
magnitudes, and whose differences of weighted contributions, exceed TOL.
3. Guarantees (exact arithmetic)
[0029] The following hold for every instance C(r,N).
[0030] (a) Single payload spike. A spike of nonzero magnitude e at position j yields s = e·H_j
and q = e·w_j. The support equals that of column j only, because the columns are distinct; the
values are uniform; and the decoder outputs REPAIRED with the payload restored.
[0031] (b) Single parity edit. An edit of magnitude f at parity row k yields s = −f·e_k and q = 0.
Every column has weight at least two, so no column matches; the confirmed decoder outputs
TAIL_EDIT and the unconfirmed decoder outputs REFUSED.
[0032] (c) Two payload spikes. Let a and b be nonzero reals, i ≠ j, and s = a·H_i + b·H_j. (c1) s
is never zero, since s_p equals a or b at any row p lying in exactly one of the two supports, and
such a row exists because the columns are distinct. (c2) s never equals a uniform multiple of a
column. If a ≠ b and a ≠ −b, the common value would have to be a or b at a row in exactly one
support, while row 0 carries a + b, which differs from both. If a = b, row 0 carries 2a while a row
in exactly one support carries a. If a = −b, row 0 carries 0, but every column contains row 0. (c3)
s has exactly one nonzero row if and only if a = −b and H_i and H_j differ in exactly one row. If
a ≠ −b, row 0 is nonzero and any other row p of H_i, which exists because H_i has weight at
least two, carries a or a + b, both nonzero, so at least two rows are nonzero. If a = −b, s = a·(H_i
− H_j), supported exactly on the rows where the columns differ.
[0033] Consequently, with the unconfirmed decoder every two-spike fault is REFUSED; with
the confirmed decoder, in case (c3) q = a·(w_i − w_j) ≠ 0, so the fault is REFUSED, and in all
other cases (c1) and (c2) give REFUSED. A decoder that instead outputs TAIL_EDIT for every
single-row syndrome without confirmation would misclassify exactly the pairs of case (c3); for
C(7,48) there are 124 such column pairs out of 1,128.

5

 [0034] (d) Same-sign faults. For k ≥ 2 spikes at distinct positions with magnitudes all strictly
positive or all strictly negative, row 0 carries the total and every other row of the union of
supports carries a nonzero partial sum, so s has at least two nonzero rows; uniformity would
require every row of the union to lie in every faulted column, contradicting distinctness. The
fault is REFUSED. For C(7,48), all 17,296 triples of distinct columns were also checked: no
combination of three columns with same-sign nonzero amplitudes equals a multiple of any
column.
[0035] (e) Disclosed boundary. Mixed-sign faults of three or more spikes can produce a
syndrome equal to a uniform multiple of a single column. Example: +1 at the columns for 11 and
13 and −1 at the column for 9 give the syndrome of column 15. Such relations are structural. For
C(7,48), 13,060 of the 17,296 triples of distinct columns have a bitwise exclusive-or equal to a
fourth column, and 7,140 of those triples admit nonzero real amplitudes a1, a2, a3 with a1·H_i +
a2·H_j + a3·H_k equal to the fourth column exactly. An exclusive-or triple (i, j, k) admits such
amplitudes exactly when one of the three supports lies between the intersection and the union of
the other two (for example S_i ∩ S_j ⊆ S_k ⊆ S_i ∪ S_j); this sandwich condition agreed with
the real-amplitude test for all 13,060 exclusive-or triples of C(7,48). Without a confirmation
value, a fault with such amplitudes would be repaired to the wrong column. With squared
weights, the confirmed decoder refused every three-spike fault in the exhaustively tested range of
section 4; this is a measured result for that range, not a proof, and mixed-sign faults of three or
more spikes remain outside the guaranteed fault model.

 ABSTRACT
A fault-refusing error-correction code family C(r,N) uses an r-by-N binary parity-check matrix
whose columns are the odd integers 3, 5, 7, and onward in increasing order, read as binary rvectors, so every column shares row 0 and has weight at least two. A repair-or-refuse decoder
repairs a single payload fault only on a unique uniform column match confirmed by a zero
recomputed syndrome, accepts a single-row syndrome as a parity edit only when an independent
confirmation value shows the payload unaltered, and otherwise refuses and records the refusal.
Every fault of two payload spikes at distinct positions, of any magnitudes and signs, is refused. A
self-describing frame format carries the parameters, lanes, payload, and parity, and a two-layer
system bars code-refused frames from per-lane headroom admission.

BACKGROUND
Field
[0003]	This disclosure relates to error-correction coding for digital communication and storage, and more particularly to codes and decoders that refuse ambiguous fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or misclassifying them.
Description of Related Art
[0004]	Conventional error-correcting codes attempt to repair every received word, mapping each syndrome to the nearest codeword. When a fault pattern is ambiguous, for example when two symbol errors combine to resemble a different single error, the decoder corrects the word to the wrong value and reports success. The corruption is silent: no flag is raised, and downstream systems act on false data.
[0005]	As one illustration, an earlier six-row design considered by the inventor, a 6-by-48 binary parity-check matrix whose columns are the first 48 six-bit vectors, in increasing integer order, having Hamming weight at least two (no row being common to all columns), silently miscorrects 56 of the 1,128 equal-magnitude, same-sign double-spike fault pairs when decoded by matching the syndrome to a uniform multiple of a single column.
[0006]	A related, less obvious failure is misclassification: a decoder that reports "parity symbol edited, payload intact" when the payload has in fact been corrupted. Such a report is as harmful as a miscorrection because the corrupted payload is accepted.
What Is Needed
[0007]	What is needed is an error-correction code family that (a) repairs unambiguous single payload faults, (b) distinguishes parity-only faults from payload faults only when that distinction is confirmed, (c) refuses ambiguous multi-fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or misclassifying them, and (d) scales across block sizes with a single constructive proof; together with a self-describing frame format and a layered refusal architecture so that refused data is barred from downstream admission decisions.
SUMMARY
[0008]	A code family C(r,N) is disclosed, where r ≥ 2 is the number of parity rows and 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1 is the number of message symbols. The r-by-N parity-check matrix H has as its columns the binary r-vectors, taken in increasing integer order with bit k of the integer giving row k, whose bit 0 is set and whose Hamming weight is at least two. Every column therefore contains a common bit (row 0).
[0009]	A repair-or-refuse decoder is disclosed. A syndrome whose support equals the support of exactly one column and whose nonzero values are all equal is repaired, and the repair is accepted only if the recomputed syndrome is zero. A syndrome supported on a single parity row is classified as a parity-tail edit only when an independent confirmation value shows that the payload is unaltered; otherwise it is refused. All other nonzero syndromes are refused and the refusal is recorded.
[0010]	Under this decoder, every fault consisting of exactly two payload spikes at distinct positions, with any nonzero real magnitudes and any signs, is refused: it is never repaired as a single spike, never reported as clean, and never reported as a parity-tail edit. Without the confirmation step or the refusal of unconfirmed single-row syndromes, two-spike faults are still never repaired as a single spike, but an equal-magnitude, opposite-sign pair at two columns that differ in exactly one row produces a single-row syndrome indistinguishable from a parity edit; the disclosed decoder therefore refuses such syndromes unless confirmed.
[0011]	A self-describing frame format (RFF-1) is disclosed, carrying the parameters (r, N), a lane count L, the payload partitioned into L lanes, and the parity H·payload. A two-layer refusal system is disclosed: the code layer admits, repairs, or refuses each frame, and a labeled-lane admission layer admits or refuses each lane of each frame that the code layer did not refuse; a frame refused at the code layer never reaches the admission layer.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION
1. Construction of C(r,N)
[0019]	Let r ≥ 2 be an integer (the number of parity rows) and let N satisfy 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1 (the number of message symbols). An integer m in 0 … 2^r − 1 is identified with the binary r-vector whose row k is bit k of m (bit 0 is the least significant bit). The parity-check matrix H (100, FIG. 1) is the r-by-N binary matrix whose j-th column (0-indexed) is the j-th such vector, taken in increasing integer order, among those with bit 0 set and Hamming weight at least two; equivalently, the odd integers 3, 5, 7, … in increasing order.
[0020]	The bound on N follows by counting: there are 2^(r−1) binary r-vectors with bit 0 set; excluding the weight-one vector (bit 0 alone) leaves 2^(r−1) − 1 admissible columns.
[0021]	Every column of H contains bit 0, shown as common-bit row 102 in FIG. 1; rows 1 through r−1 are shown as rows 104 and the columns as columns 106. Example: C(7,48) is the [55,48] code with 7 parity rows protecting 48 message symbols; its columns are the odd integers 3 through 97.
2. Decoder
[0022]	Referring to FIG. 3, given a received word with payload estimate v′ (N real values) and parity estimate t′ (r real values), and, in the confirmed embodiment, a received confirmation symbol u′, the decoder performs the following steps.
[0023]	(i) Step 302: compute the syndrome s = H·v′ − t′.
[0024]	(ii) Step 304: in the confirmed embodiment, compute the confirmation residual q = Σ_j w_j·v′_j − u′, where w_0 … w_(N−1) are pairwise distinct nonzero weights and the transmitted confirmation symbol is u = Σ_j w_j·v_j. In a preferred embodiment w_j = (j + 1)^2. The weights are preferably not an affine function of the column integer: because the column vectors are binary, any relation a·H_i + b·H_j + c·H_k = d·H_l among columns also holds among the column integers, so weights affine in the column integer (for example w_j = j + 1, which equals (m_j − 1)/2 for column integer m_j) give no additional protection against such relations, whereas squared weights did in the tested range (section 4).
[0025]	(iii) Step 306: if every component of s is zero and q is zero, output CLEAN (308). If s is zero and q is nonzero, output CONFIRMATION_EDIT: the confirmation symbol alone was altered and the payload passes all r parity checks.
[0026]	(iv) Step 310: let supp(s) be the set of rows where s is nonzero. If supp(s) equals the support of exactly one column j, all nonzero components of s equal a common value c, and (in the confirmed embodiment) q = c·w_j, subtract c from v′_j, recompute the syndrome, and output REPAIRED (312) only if the recomputed syndrome is zero; otherwise output REFUSED.
[0027]	(v) Step 314: if supp(s) is a single row k, then in the confirmed embodiment (step 316) output TAIL_EDIT (318, payload intact) only if q = 0 and otherwise output REFUSED; in the unconfirmed embodiment output REFUSED, the parity fault being detected but the payload not accepted.
[0028]	(vi) Step 320: otherwise output REFUSED, store a refusal record (322) comprising at least the syndrome, and take no corrective action.
[0029]	"Zero" in a floating-point implementation means magnitude not exceeding a tolerance TOL fixed in advance (for example 1e−9 relative to the largest payload magnitude). The guarantees of section 3 are stated for exact arithmetic and hold in floating point for faults whose magnitudes, and whose differences of weighted contributions, exceed TOL.
3. Guarantees (exact arithmetic)
[0030]	The following hold for every instance C(r,N).
[0031]	(a) Single payload spike. A spike of nonzero magnitude e at position j yields s = e·H_j and q = e·w_j. The support equals that of column j only, because the columns are distinct; the values are uniform; and the decoder outputs REPAIRED with the payload restored.
[0032]	(b) Single parity edit. An edit of magnitude f at parity row k yields s = −f·e_k and q = 0. Every column has weight at least two, so no column matches; the confirmed decoder outputs TAIL_EDIT and the unconfirmed decoder outputs REFUSED.
[0033]	(c) Two payload spikes. Let a and b be nonzero reals, i ≠ j, and s = a·H_i + b·H_j. (c1) s is never zero, since s_p equals a or b at any row p lying in exactly one of the two supports, and such a row exists because the columns are distinct. (c2) s never equals a uniform multiple of a column. If a ≠ b and a ≠ −b, the common value would have to be a or b at a row in exactly one support, while row 0 carries a + b, which differs from both. If a = b, row 0 carries 2a while a row in exactly one support carries a. If a = −b, row 0 carries 0, but every column contains row 0. (c3) s has exactly one nonzero row if and only if a = −b and H_i and H_j differ in exactly one row. If a ≠ −b, row 0 is nonzero and any other row p of H_i, which exists because H_i has weight at least two, carries a or a + b, both nonzero, so at least two rows are nonzero. If a = −b, s = a·(H_i − H_j), supported exactly on the rows where the columns differ.
[0034]	Consequently, with the unconfirmed decoder every two-spike fault is REFUSED; with the confirmed decoder, in case (c3) q = a·(w_i − w_j) ≠ 0, so the fault is REFUSED, and in all other cases (c1) and (c2) give REFUSED. A decoder that instead outputs TAIL_EDIT for every single-row syndrome without confirmation would misclassify exactly the pairs of case (c3); for C(7,48) there are 124 such column pairs out of 1,128. FIG. 7 shows the smallest instance: in C(3,3) the columns are 3 = rows {0,1} (702), 5 = rows {0,2} (704), and 7 = rows {0,1,2} (706) in the support lattice 700; spikes +e at column 3 and −e at column 7 give s = (0, 0, −e), a single-row syndrome on row 2 (708), and columns 5 and 7 likewise give a single-row syndrome on row 1, whereas columns 3 and 5 differ in two rows and give a two-row syndrome.
[0035]	(d) Same-sign faults. For k ≥ 2 spikes at distinct positions with magnitudes all strictly positive or all strictly negative, row 0 carries the total and every other row of the union of supports carries a nonzero partial sum, so s has at least two nonzero rows; uniformity would require every row of the union to lie in every faulted column, contradicting distinctness. The fault is REFUSED. For C(7,48), all 17,296 triples of distinct columns were also checked: no combination of three columns with same-sign nonzero amplitudes equals a multiple of any column.
[0036]	(e) Disclosed boundary. Mixed-sign faults of three or more spikes can produce a syndrome equal to a uniform multiple of a single column. Example: +1 at the columns for 11 and 13 and −1 at the column for 9 give the syndrome of column 15. Such relations are structural. For C(7,48), 13,060 of the 17,296 triples of distinct columns have a bitwise exclusive-or equal to a fourth column, and 7,140 of those triples admit nonzero real amplitudes a1, a2, a3 with a1·H_i + a2·H_j + a3·H_k equal to the fourth column exactly. An exclusive-or triple (i, j, k) admits such amplitudes exactly when one of the three supports lies between the intersection and the union of the other two (for example S_i ∩ S_j ⊆ S_k ⊆ S_i ∪ S_j); this sandwich condition agreed with the real-amplitude test for all 13,060 exclusive-or triples of C(7,48). Without a confirmation value, a fault with such amplitudes would be repaired to the wrong column. With squared weights, the confirmed decoder refused every three-spike fault in the exhaustively tested range of section 4; this is a measured result for that range, not a proof, and mixed-sign faults of three or more spikes remain outside the guaranteed fault model.
4. Verification

Counts below are summed over every N for each r.
[0038]	Two-spike faults, 24,871,680 events in total: a decoder that accepts every single-row syndrome as a parity edit gave 0 miscorrections and 240,840 misclassifications; the unconfirmed decoder (single-row syndromes refused) gave 0 and 0; the confirmed decoder gave 0 and 0.
[0039]	Three-spike faults, 2,449,705,032 events in total: a decoder that accepts every single-row syndrome gave 23,903,280 miscorrections and 276,948 misclassifications; the unconfirmed decoder gave 23,903,280 and 0; the confirmed decoder with w_j = j + 1 gave 23,903,280 and 276,948; the confirmed decoder with w_j = (j + 1)^2 gave 0 and 0. No fault in either battery produced a zero syndrome.
[0040]	For C(7,48): every single spike is repaired; every single parity edit is classified; all 1,128 equal-magnitude same-sign pairs are refused; of the 1,128 equal-magnitude opposite-sign pairs, 124 produce a single-row syndrome and are refused by both disclosed decoders, and 1,004 produce a multi-row syndrome without row 0 and are refused.
5. RFF-1 Self-Describing Frame Format
[0041]	Referring to FIG. 4, a frame 400 comprises, in order: a magic field 402 of 4 bytes, value 0x52464631 (ASCII "RFF1"); a field 404 of 1 byte giving the parity-row count r, 2 ≤ r; a field 406 of 2 bytes, unsigned big-endian, giving the message-symbol count N, 1 ≤ N ≤ 2^(r−1) − 1; a field 408 of 1 byte giving the lane count L, 1 ≤ L, where L divides N; a payload 410 of N IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, where lane l (0-indexed) holds symbols l·N/L through (l+1)·N/L − 1; a parity field 412 of r IEEE-754 binary64 values, big-endian, equal to H·payload; and, in the confirmed embodiment, a confirmation field 414 of one further IEEE-754 binary64 value u = Σ_j w_j·payload_j, with w_j = j + 1 unless otherwise signaled.
[0042]	In a version-2 variant, the magic field is 0xD2464631 (0x52464631 with bit 31 set) and the payload, parity, and confirmation values are IEEE-754 binary32; a receiver implementing only version 1 refuses a frame whose magic field it does not recognize.
[0043]	A receiver parses the header, reconstructs H from (r, N) by the construction of section 1, and decodes the frame per section 2. A header with r, N, or L outside the stated ranges is refused.
6. Two-Layer Refusal System
[0044]	Referring to FIG. 5, in Layer 1 (code layer 502) each received frame from channel 500 is decoded per section 2, yielding CLEAN, REPAIRED, TAIL_EDIT, CONFIRMATION_EDIT, or REFUSED. Frames output as REFUSED are recorded in refusal store 504 and are not passed to Layer 2. Frames output as REPAIRED are passed with the corrected payload; frames output as CLEAN, TAIL_EDIT, or CONFIRMATION_EDIT are passed with the received payload.
[0045]	In Layer 2 (admission layer 506), each frame passed by Layer 1 is partitioned into its L lanes. For each lane, a claimed figure C_i and an interior figure I_i are retained under a label i unique within the lane's record, a label-specific headroom H_i = I_i − C_i is computed, and the lane is admitted (508) only if every required label has a corresponding interior label and H_i ≥ 0 for every required label; otherwise the lane is refused (510). A surplus at one label or lane is not applied to a deficit at another label or lane. Each admission or refusal is written as a new decision record without overwriting the input records (see U.S. Provisional Application No. 64/169,264).
7. Instances and Overhead
[0046]	Referring to FIG. 6, the following instances were constructed: C(6,31), a [37,31] code with overhead 16.2%, 465 column pairs, of which 75 differ in exactly one row; C(7,48), a [55,48] code with overhead 12.7%, 1,128 pairs, 124 differing in one row; C(7,63), a [70,63] code with overhead 10.0%, 1,953 pairs, 186 differing in one row; C(8,100), a [108,100] code with overhead 7.4%, 4,950 pairs, 312 differing in one row; C(8,127), a [135,127] code with overhead 5.9%, 8,001 pairs, 441 differing in one row; C(9,255), a [264,255] code with overhead 3.4%, 32,385 pairs, 1,016 differing in one row; and C(10,511), a [521,511] code with overhead 1.9%, 130,305 pairs, 2,295 differing in one row. Overhead is r/(N+r).
[0047]	The pairs differing in exactly one row are those whose equal-magnitude opposite-sign faults produce single-row syndromes; all of them are refused by both disclosed decoders. The confirmed embodiment adds one symbol, giving overhead (r+1)/(N+r+1); for C(7,48), 8/56 = 14.3%.
8. Alternative Embodiments
[0048]	(a) Even-weight construction: columns with bit 0 set whose remaining bits have nonzero even weight. Any two such columns differ in at least two rows, so case (c3) cannot occur and no confirmation symbol is needed; the capacity is 2^(r−2) − 1 columns (for 48 columns, r = 8).
[0049]	(b) Column orderings other than increasing integer order, provided the common-bit and weight properties are preserved.
[0050]	(c) Confirmation by an independent check other than a weighted sum, for example a cryptographic digest of the payload, in which case a single-row syndrome is classified TAIL_EDIT only if the digest verifies.
[0051]	(d) The operations may be performed by a fixed-function datapath in which H is stored in read-only memory, the syndrome is computed by parallel multiply-accumulate units, the column match is performed by a support lookup, and the refusal output is a signal that gates downstream dispatch. The operations may also be performed by a general-purpose processor executing instructions stored on a non-transitory computer-readable medium, by a field-programmable gate array, or by an application-specific integrated circuit.
[0052]	(e) Dependency-aware column selection. Because the common-bit and weight properties hold for any N distinct admissible columns, the two-spike guarantees of section 3(c) hold for any such selection, and the columns may be chosen from the 2^(r−1) − 1 admissible vectors to reduce the number of sandwich triples of section 3(e), for example by greedy local search or simulated annealing. For r = 7 and N = 48, the following 48 columns (each written as a 7-bit binary number with bit 0 as least significant bit) have 5,452 sandwich triples, compared with 7,140 for the increasing-order selection, a 23.6% reduction; this selection has 101 column pairs that differ in exactly one row, each refused under section 2(v): 0000011, 0000101, 0000111, 0001001, 0001101, 0001111, 0010001, 0010101, 0010111, 0011001, 0011011, 0011111, 0100001, 0100011, 0100101, 0101011, 0101101, 0101111, 0110001, 0110011, 0110101, 0111001, 0111011, 0111111, 1000001, 1000011, 1001001, 1001101, 1001111, 1010011, 1010101, 1010111, 1011001, 1011011, 1011101, 1100001, 1100011, 1100101, 1100111, 1101001, 1101011, 1101111, 1110011, 1110101, 1110111, 1111001, 1111101, 1111111.
[0053]	(f) Adaptive tolerance. The tolerance TOL of section 2 may be set from a measured channel noise floor as TOL = κ·σ, where σ is an estimated per-symbol noise standard deviation and κ ≥ 3 is a confidence factor.
9. Industrial Applicability
[0054]	The family is applicable to any digital link or storage medium where silent data corruption is costlier than retransmission or erasure, including radio links, satellite command links, sensor feeds, and autonomous-system sensor buses.

ABSTRACT
A fault-refusing error-correction code family C(r,N) uses an r-by-N binary parity-check matrix whose columns are the odd integers 3, 5, 7, and onward in increasing order, read as binary r-vectors, so every column shares row 0 and has weight at least two. A repair-or-refuse decoder repairs a single payload fault only on a unique uniform column match confirmed by a zero recomputed syndrome, accepts a single-row syndrome as a parity edit only when an independent confirmation value shows the payload unaltered, and otherwise refuses and records the refusal. Every fault of two payload spikes at distinct positions, of any magnitudes and signs, is refused. A self-describing frame format carries the parameters, lanes, payload, and parity, and a two-layer system bars code-refused frames from per-lane headroom admission.

BACKGROUND
Field
[0003] This disclosure relates to error-correction coding for digital communication and storage,
and more particularly to codes and decoders that refuse ambiguous fault patterns instead of
miscorrecting or misclassifying them.
Description of Related Art
[0004] Conventional error-correcting codes attempt to repair every received word, mapping each
syndrome to the nearest codeword. When a fault pattern is ambiguous, for example when two
symbol errors combine to resemble a different single error, the decoder corrects the word to the
wrong value and reports success. The corruption is silent: no flag is raised, and downstream
systems act on false data.
[0005] As one illustration, an earlier six-row design considered by the inventor, a 6-by-48 binary
parity-check matrix whose columns are the first 48 six-bit vectors, in increasing integer order,
having Hamming weight at least two (no row being common to all columns), silently miscorrects

1

 56 of the 1,128 equal-magnitude, same-sign double-spike fault pairs when decoded by matching
the syndrome to a uniform multiple of a single column.
[0006] A related, less obvious failure is misclassification: a decoder that reports "parity symbol
edited, payload intact" when the payload has in fact been corrupted. Such a report is as harmful
as a miscorrection because the corrupted payload is accepted.
What Is Needed
[0007] What is needed is an error-correction code family that (a) repairs unambiguous single
payload faults, (b) distinguishes parity-only faults from payload faults only when that distinction
is confirmed, (c) refuses ambiguous multi-fault patterns instead of miscorrecting or
misclassifying them, and (d) scales across block sizes with a single constructive proof; together
with a self-describing frame format and a layered refusal architecture so that refused data is
barred from downstream admission decisions.
SUMMARY
[0008] A code family C(r,N) is disclosed, where r ≥ 2 is the number of parity rows and 1 ≤ N ≤
2^(r−1) − 1 is the number of message symbols. The r-by-N parity-check matrix H has as its
columns the binary r-vectors, taken in increasing integer order with bit k of the integer giving
row k, whose bit 0 is set and whose Hamming weight is at least two. Every column therefore
contains a common bit (row 0).
[0009] A repair-or-refuse decoder is disclosed. A syndrome whose support equals the support of
exactly one column and whose nonzero values are all equal is repaired, and the repair is accepted
only if the recomputed syndrome is zero. A syndrome supported on a single parity row is
classified as a parity-tail edit only when an independent confirmation value shows that the
payload is unaltered; otherwise it is refused. All other nonzero syndromes are refused and the
refusal is recorded.
[0010] Under this decoder, every fault consisting of exactly two payload spikes at distinct
positions, with any nonzero real magnitudes and any signs, is refused: it is never repaired as a
single spike, never reported as clean, and never reported as a parity-tail edit. Without the
confirmation step or the refusal of unconfirmed single-row syndromes, two-spike faults are still
never repaired as a single spike, but an equal-magnitude, opposite-sign pair at two columns that

2

 differ in exactly one row produces a single-row syndrome indistinguishable from a parity edit;
the disclosed decoder therefore refuses such syndromes unless confirmed.
[0011] A self-describing frame format (RFF-1) is disclosed, carrying the parameters (r, N), a
lane count L, the payload partitioned into L lanes, and the parity H·payload. A two-layer refusal
system is disclosed: the code layer admits, repairs, or refuses each frame, and a labeled-lane
admission layer admits or refuses each lane of each frame that the code layer did not refuse; a
frame refused at the code layer never reaches the admission layer.
